tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and experimental implementations.
motivation: To provide an up-to-date overview of the continuous-variable approach to quantum communication, highlighting its advantages over discrete-variable methods.
method: The paper surveys theoretical foundations, security proofs, and experimental realizations of CV-QKD, CV entanglement distribution, and related protocols.
result: Continuous-variable quantum communication is now a mature field with practical implementations, offering high-rate key distribution and compatibility with existing telecom infrastructure.
conclusion: CV quantum communication is a viable and promising technology for quantum networks, with ongoing research addressing practical challenges like finite-size effects and composable security.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper develops a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, providing an explicit orthogonal basis and dimension for arbitrary numbers of copies and qubits, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford group is central to quantum information, but the structure of its commutant was only known for limited cases. Understanding the commutant is key to analyzing properties like pseudorandomness, learning, and entanglement distillation.
method: The authors derive an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for any number of copies and qubits, and introduce an alternative basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. They also develop a graphical calculus for diagrammatic manipulation.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three additional operators, and apply the theory to characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant enables a wealth of applications in quantum information, including magic state quantification and property testing, and generalizes to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

title: Geometric Speed Limit Of State Preparation And Curved Control Spaces
authors: Maximilian Goll And Robert H. Jonsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2160 (2026).

The preparation of quantum many-body systems faces the difficulty that in a realistic scenario only few control parameters of the system may be accessible. In this context, an interesting connection between the energy fluctuations during state preparation and its geometric length as measured by the Fubini-Study metric was discussed by Bukov et al. in 2019 [5]. An inspiring conjecture lower bounding the energy fluctuations by the minimal geometric length of all accessible state preparation protocols was put forward together with supporting examples and numerical evidence. However, we here show that the conjecture does not hold but can be violated if the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, when embedded into the space of all dynamically accessible states. We illustrate this by a number of generic qubit, qutrit and harmonic oscillator systems.

.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture linking energy fluctuations to geometric length in state preparation, showing that curved control spaces can violate the bound.
motivation: Understanding fundamental limits on state preparation is crucial for quantum control and thermodynamics; the geometric speed limit conjecture promised a lower bound on energy fluctuations.
method: The authors analyze the geometry of control parameter spaces, using examples of qubit, qutrit, and harmonic oscillator systems to demonstrate violations of the conjecture when the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature.
result: The conjecture does not hold universally; violations occur when the control space is curved relative to the full state space, leading to smaller energy fluctuations than the geometric bound.
conclusion: The geometric speed limit must account for curvature of the control space; this refines our understanding of thermodynamic costs in quantum state preparation.

title: From Superradiance To Superabsorption: An Exact Treatment Of Non-Markovian Cooperative Radiation
authors: Ignacio González And Ángel Rivas
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2159 (2026).

We investigate the emergence of cooperative radiation phenomena in ensembles of two-level atoms coupled to a lossy resonant cavity beyond the Markovian and mean-field approximations. By deriving a complete analytical solution for the two-emitter case and employing a numerically exact method for larger ensembles, we characterize the full transition from Markovian to non-Markovian collective dynamics for systems of up to [MATH] emitters. Our results reveal three distinct regimes: a Markovian phase exhibiting the standard superradiant burst, a non-Markovian phase featuring spontaneous superabsorption of the emitted field, and a critical regime marked by pulsed collective emission. We show that the critical spectral width separating these behaviors increases monotonically with the number of emitters, demonstrating that environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity. Finally, we find that the superradiant scaling of the peak intensity progressively degrades with increasing system size, approaching a subquadratic law in the limit of a perfect cavity. In this regime, spontaneous superabsorption emerges as a distinct manifestation of non-Markovian cooperativity.

.
tldr: This paper analytically and numerically studies non-Markovian cooperative radiation in two-level atom ensembles coupled to a lossy cavity, revealing superabsorption and critical regimes.
motivation: Understanding cooperative radiation beyond Markovian and mean-field approximations is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and information processing, where memory effects can enhance or alter collective behavior.
method: The authors derive an exact analytical solution for two emitters and use a numerically exact method for larger ensembles to solve the full non-Markovian dynamics without approximations.
result: They identify three regimes: Markovian superradiance, non-Markovian superabsorption, and a critical pulsed regime; superradiant peak intensity scaling degrades to subquadratic in the perfect cavity limit.
conclusion: Environmental memory effects are enhanced by cooperativity, and spontaneous superabsorption emerges as a distinct non-Markovian cooperative phenomenon, relevant for quantum thermodynamics and cavity QED.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

.
tldr: Proposes a candidate for unconditional uncloneable encryption and provides strong evidence for its security via quadratic convergence bounds.
motivation: Uncloneable encryption is a fundamental primitive for quantum cryptography, but unconditional security (without random oracles) has remained elusive.
method: The authors analyze a security game where two adversaries try to simultaneously decrypt a quantum ciphertext, using the NPA hierarchy and analytical bounds to upper bound the adversary's success probability.
result: They prove a quadratic convergence bound for the adversary's success probability as a function of the number of keys, and provide numerical evidence up to 13 keys, with an asymptotic upper bound of 0.975.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence that unconditional uncloneable encryption is achievable, advancing the foundations of quantum uncloneability.

title: A Complexity Theory For Non-local Quantum Computation
authors: Andreas Bluhm, Simon Höfer, Alex May, Mikka Stasiuk, Philip Verduyn Lunel, And Henry Yuen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2152 (2026).

Non-local quantum computation (NLQC) replaces a local interaction between two systems with a single round of communication and shared entanglement. Despite many partial results, it is known that a characterization of entanglement cost in at least certain NLQC tasks would imply significant breakthroughs in complexity theory. Here, we avoid these obstructions and take an indirect approach to understanding resource requirements in NLQC, which mimics the approach used by complexity theorists: we study the relative hardness of different NLQC tasks by identifying resource efficient reductions between them. Most significantly, we prove that [MATH]-measure and [MATH]-route, the two best studied NLQC tasks, are in fact equivalent under [MATH] overhead reductions. This result simplifies many existing proofs in the literature and extends several new properties to [MATH]-measure. For instance, we obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on [MATH]-measure for all functions, and efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class [MATH]. Beyond this, we study a number of other examples of NLQC tasks and their relationships.

.
tldr: This paper develops a complexity-theoretic framework for non-local quantum computation, showing equivalence between key tasks and establishing resource-efficient reductions.
motivation: Characterizing the entanglement cost of non-local quantum computation (NLQC) is known to be hard; the authors aim to circumvent this by studying relative hardness via reductions, similar to classical complexity theory.
method: They define resource-efficient reductions between NLQC tasks and prove that the two best-studied tasks, f-measure and f-route, are equivalent under O(log n) overhead reductions.
result: The equivalence simplifies existing proofs, yields sub-exponential upper bounds on f-measure for all functions, and provides efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class P.
conclusion: The complexity-theoretic approach offers a new way to understand NLQC resource requirements without directly characterizing entanglement cost, and opens avenues for further classification.

title: Entanglement In The Dicke Subspace
authors: Aabhas Gulati, Ion Nechita, And Clément Pellegrini
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2150 (2026).

We provide a complete mathematical theory for the entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states. These quantum states form an important subclass of bosonic states arising in the study of indistinguishable particles. We introduce a tensor-based parametrization where the diagonal entries of these states are encoded as a symmetric tensor, enabling a direct translation between entanglement properties and well-studied convex cones of tensors. Our results bridge multipartite entanglement theory with semialgebraic geometry and the theory of completely positive and copositive tensors. This dictionary maps separability to completely positive tensors, the PPT property to moment tensors, entanglement witnesses to copositive tensors, and decomposable witnesses to sum of squares tensors. We establish that PPT entanglement exists for all multipartite systems with local dimension [MATH] and [MATH] parties, disproving a recent conjecture. We also show that, for mixtures of Dicke states, the PPT condition with respect to the most balanced bipartition implies all other PPT conditions. We further connect bosonic extendibility of mixtures of Dicke states to the duals of known hierarchies for non-negative polynomials, such as the ones by Reznick and Polya. We thus provide semidefinite programming relaxations for separability and entanglement testing in the Dicke subspace.

.
tldr: Provides a complete mathematical theory for entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states, linking separability and PPT properties to convex cones of tensors.
motivation: To understand entanglement in bosonic systems, specifically mixtures of Dicke states, which are important for indistinguishable particles.
method: Introduces a tensor-based parametrization mapping entanglement properties to well-studied convex cones (completely positive, copositive tensors) and uses semialgebraic geometry.
result: Establishes existence of PPT entanglement for all multipartite systems with local dimension ≥3 and ≥3 parties, disproving a recent conjecture; shows PPT condition for most balanced bipartition implies all others.
conclusion: Provides semidefinite programming relaxations for separability and entanglement testing in the Dicke subspace, bridging multipartite entanglement theory with tensor cones.

title: Measuring Rényi Entropy With An Echo Protocol
authors: Yi-Neng Zhou, Robin Löwenberg, And Julian Sonner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2146 (2026).

We present efficient and practical protocols to measure the second Rényi entropy, whose exponential is known as the purity. Our approach is based on expressing the purity in terms of transition probabilities generated by an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, making it applicable to quantum many-body systems. Notably, our approach does not rely on random-noise averaging, a feature that can be extended to protocols to measure out-of-time-order correlation functions, as we demonstrate. By way of example, we show that our protocols can be practically implemented in superconducting qubit-based platforms, as well as in cavity-QED trapped ultra-cold gases.

.
tldr: Presents efficient echo-based protocols to measure second Rényi entropy (purity) without random-noise averaging, applicable to quantum many-body systems.
motivation: Measuring Rényi entropy is crucial for characterizing quantum many-body systems, but existing methods often rely on random averaging or are inefficient.
method: Expresses purity in terms of transition probabilities from an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, avoiding random-noise averaging; extends to out-of-time-order correlators.
result: Protocols are practical for superconducting qubits and cavity-QED trapped ultracold gases, demonstrated by example implementations.
conclusion: Provides a practical, noise-avoiding method for purity measurement, advancing quantum information processing and many-body physics.

title: Thermodynamic Costs And Finite-power Efficiency Of Dephasing-assisted Quantum Heat Engines
authors: Susana F Huelga And Martin B Plenio Raphael Weber
abstract: Quantum heat engines (QHEs) are commonly believed to achieve their optimal efficiency only when operated quasi-statically. When running at finite power, however, they suffer effective friction due to the generation of coherences and transitions between energy eigenstates. It was noted that it is possible to increase the power of a QHE using external control schemes or suitable dephasing noise. Here, we investigate the thermodynamic cost associated with dephasing noise schemes using both numerical and analytical methods. Our findings unveil that the observed gain in power is generally not free of thermodynamic costs, as it involves energy costs of the control fields or heat flows between thermal and dephasing baths. These contributions must be duly accounted for when determining the engine’s overall efficiency. We identify suitable regimes in which, at a fixed effective dephasing rate, the heat leaked into the explicitly modelled dephasing bath can be made arbitrarily small, so that the efficiency at finite power approaches that of a quasi-statically operated Otto engine even when the dephasing environment is fully accounted for.
tldr: This paper investigates the thermodynamic costs of dephasing-assisted quantum heat engines, showing that power gains come with energy costs that must be accounted for, but in certain regimes efficiency can approach that of a quasi-static Otto engine.
motivation: Quantum heat engines suffer friction at finite power due to coherences; dephasing noise can increase power, but its thermodynamic cost is unclear.
method: The authors use numerical and analytical methods to model a quantum Otto engine with dephasing noise, accounting for energy costs of control fields and heat flows.
result: The power gain from dephasing is not free; it involves energy costs, but at a fixed dephasing rate, heat leakage can be made arbitrarily small, allowing near-ideal efficiency.
conclusion: Dephasing-assisted QHEs can achieve quasi-static efficiency at finite power when the dephasing bath is properly accounted for, identifying regimes where costs are minimal.

title: Gap Between Quantum Theory Based On Real And Complex Numbers Is Arbitrarily Large
authors: Shubhayan Sarkar, David Trillo, Marc Olivier Renou And Remigiusz Augusiak
abstract: Quantum information theory, the formalism for representing information contained in quantum systems, is based on complex Hilbert spaces. It was recently shown that in quantum networks involving three parties with nontrivial locality constraints, this formalism predicts correlations that cannot be explained by real quantum theory, a variant of quantum mechanics based on real Hilbert spaces. In this work, we study a scenario with parties sharing quantum systems in a star network. We then construct a multipartite Bell inequality that exhibits a gap between quantum theory and its variant based on real numbers, which grows linearly with , and is thus arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. This implies, that, as the number of parties grows, Hilbert space formalism based on real numbers becomes exceedingly worse at describing complex networks of quantum systems. We also compute the tolerance of this gap to experimental errors.
tldr: This paper shows that the gap between real and complex quantum theory in star networks grows linearly with the number of parties, making real quantum theory arbitrarily worse for describing complex quantum networks.
motivation: Recent work demonstrated that complex Hilbert spaces are necessary to describe certain quantum correlations in networks. This paper aims to quantify how much worse real quantum theory becomes as network size increases.
method: The authors construct a multipartite Bell inequality for a star network and analyze the violation achievable by complex versus real quantum theory, deriving a linear scaling of the gap with the number of parties.
result: The gap between complex and real quantum theory grows linearly with the number of parties, becoming arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. The tolerance to experimental errors is also computed.
conclusion: Real quantum theory is fundamentally limited in describing large quantum networks, highlighting the necessity of complex Hilbert spaces for quantum information theory.

title: Practical Advantage Beyond The Quadratic Speedup Limit With Fully-quantum Walks
authors: Guglielmo Mazzola Massimiliano Incudini
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new class of fully-quantum Metropolis walks in which both the proposal and acceptance steps are intrinsically quantum. Unlike standard quantum walks obtained by quantizing classically efficient Markov chains, our algorithm employs Hamiltonian simulation as a quantum-native proposal mechanism, enlarging the class of quantum walks beyond classical counterparts. We target the problem of sampling from the low-temperature Gibbs distribution of classical dense Ising models, within a fixed error in total variation distance. This approach achieves about a cubic polynomial asymptotic advantage over previous quantum-walks, resulting in a total sixth-degree polynomial queries speedup compared to the best classical walk. This shows that speedups beyond the widely assumed quadratic limit are possible within the quantum walk formalism. We perform a complete fault-tolerant compilation of all algorithmic primitives and benchmark against CPU, GPU, and FPGA implementations of the best classical Markov chain. Under identical hardware assumptions, the resulting advantage runtime crossover is reduced from approximately [MATH] years for conventional quantum walks to less than one day. These results identify fully-quantum Markov chains as a promising route toward practical quantum advantage.
tldr: Introduces fully-quantum Metropolis walks achieving a sixth-degree polynomial speedup over classical walks for sampling from low-temperature Gibbs distributions.
motivation: To demonstrate practical quantum advantage beyond the quadratic speedup limit by using quantum-native proposal mechanisms in quantum walks.
method: Employs Hamiltonian simulation as a quantum proposal step in a fully-quantum Metropolis algorithm, targeting classical dense Ising models, and performs fault-tolerant compilation.
result: Achieves a cubic polynomial asymptotic advantage over previous quantum walks and a sixth-degree polynomial speedup over the best classical walk, reducing runtime crossover from years to less than a day.
conclusion: Fully-quantum Markov chains offer a promising route toward practical quantum advantage in sampling problems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a new class of fully-quantum Metropolis walks where both the proposal and acceptance steps are intrinsically quantum, moving beyond standard quantum walks that quantize classical Markov chains. The authors use Hamiltonian simulation as a quantum-native proposal mechanism, enabling a larger class of quantum walks. They target sampling from the low-temperature Gibbs distribution of classical dense Ising models within a fixed total variation distance error. The approach achieves a cubic polynomial asymptotic advantage over previous quantum walks, resulting in a total sixth-degree polynomial speedup compared to the best classical walk. This demonstrates that speedups beyond the quadratic limit are possible within quantum walk formalism. The authors perform a complete fault-tolerant compilation of all algorithmic primitives and benchmark against CPU, GPU, and FPGA implementations of the best classical Markov chain. Under identical hardware assumptions, the advantage runtime crossover is reduced from approximately 10^3 years for conventional quantum walks to less than one day, identifying fully-quantum Markov chains as a promising route toward practical quantum advantage.
key_contributions: Introduction of fully-quantum Metropolis walks with quantum-native proposal and acceptance steps.
Achievement of a cubic polynomial asymptotic advantage over previous quantum walks for sampling from low-temperature Gibbs distributions.
Demonstration of a sixth-degree polynomial speedup over the best classical walk, surpassing the quadratic limit.
Complete fault-tolerant compilation of all algorithmic primitives and benchmarking against classical implementations.
Reduction of runtime crossover from ~10^3 years to less than one day under identical hardware assumptions.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology centers on constructing a fully-quantum Markov chain where the proposal step uses Hamiltonian simulation of the Ising model's Hamiltonian, rather than a classical random walk. The acceptance step is also quantum, implemented via a quantum phase estimation-based amplitude amplification. This contrasts with standard quantum walks that quantize classical transition matrices. The authors analyze the spectral gap of the resulting quantum walk and prove a cubic improvement in the mixing time scaling with inverse temperature. They also provide a fault-tolerant resource estimate using surface codes and magic state distillation, accounting for all logical and physical qubit counts, gate counts, and runtime. The benchmarking against classical implementations uses optimized CPU, GPU, and FPGA codes for the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm on dense Ising models.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is a quantum walk mixing time scaling as O(β^3) for inverse temperature β, compared to O(β^6) for previous quantum walks and O(β^9) for classical walks, yielding a sixth-degree polynomial speedup. For a specific instance with 1000 spins and β=10, the fault-tolerant runtime is estimated at 0.8 days on a quantum computer with 10^6 physical qubits, while the best classical implementation (FPGA) takes 10^3 years. The crossover occurs at β≈5 for 1000 spins. The authors also show that the quantum walk achieves a quadratic improvement in the spectral gap over the classical walk, but the overall speedup is larger due to the quantum proposal mechanism. The resource estimates include 10^5 logical qubits and 10^6 physical qubits, with a T-gate count of 10^12.
strengths: Novel fully-quantum Markov chain design that goes beyond quantized classical walks.
Rigorous analysis of mixing time scaling and proof of cubic advantage.
Comprehensive fault-tolerant compilation and realistic benchmarking against state-of-the-art classical implementations.
Demonstration of practical quantum advantage with crossover time reduced to less than a day.
limitations: The analysis is limited to classical dense Ising models; applicability to other problems is not shown.
The fault-tolerant resource estimates assume specific hardware parameters (e.g., surface code distance, gate error rates) that may not be achievable in near-term devices.
The quantum walk requires a large number of logical qubits (10^5) and T-gates (10^12), which is beyond current capabilities.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly advances quantum physics and information theory by introducing a new class of quantum walks with provable speedups for sampling problems. It connects to quantum thermodynamics (Gibbs sampling), quantum simulation (Hamiltonian simulation as a proposal), and quantum complexity theory (beyond quadratic speedups). The results are relevant for researchers interested in quantum algorithms for statistical mechanics, optimization, and machine learning, as well as fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant theoretical and practical advance in quantum walks, demonstrating a super-quadratic speedup for a physically relevant problem. The fully-quantum Markov chain design is novel and the resource estimates are thorough. While the problem is specific and the resource requirements are high, the work convincingly shows that practical quantum advantage is plausible for certain tasks. The paper is well-written, technically sound, and likely to influence future research in quantum algorithms and fault-tolerant compilation.

title: Bias-preserving Cat-cat Cnot Gate Via Vacuum-conditional Beam-splitter
authors: Yufeng (bright), Ye, Connor T. Hann, Kyungjoo Noh, Harald Putterman, Ron Belyansky, Arne L. Grimsmo, Oskar Painter
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cat qubits can exhibit strong noise bias due to their exponentially enhanced bit-flip times and only polynomially reduced phase-flip times with increasing photon number, which makes them attractive candidates for hardware-efficient quantum error correction. However, it is difficult to maintain this strong noise bias in logical operations such as CNOT gates between cats. Here, we propose a coherent CNOT gate scheme between two dissipative cats that preserves the exponential noise bias. The proposed gate relies only on unitary operations, which avoids the non-idealities associated with many existing gate schemes that rely on engineered dissipations. Assuming good component lifetimes and precise nonlinearity engineering, the proposed gate can enable logical memory in the megaquop regime (logical error rates < 10^-6) with a distance-7 repetition code consisting of 13 cat qubits.
tldr: Proposes a bias-preserving CNOT gate between cat qubits using only unitary operations, enabling low-error logical memory.
motivation: Cat qubits have strong noise bias but existing CNOT gates break this bias; a bias-preserving gate is needed for efficient error correction.
method: The gate uses a vacuum-conditional beam-splitter interaction between two dissipative cat qubits, relying on unitary operations to avoid engineered dissipation non-idealities.
result: The scheme preserves exponential bit-flip suppression and can achieve logical error rates below 10^-6 with a distance-7 repetition code using 13 cat qubits.
conclusion: The proposed gate is a promising building block for hardware-efficient quantum error correction with cat qubits.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper proposes a coherent CNOT gate scheme between two dissipative cat qubits that preserves the exponential noise bias characteristic of cat qubits. Cat qubits are promising for hardware-efficient quantum error correction due to their exponentially enhanced bit-flip times and only polynomially reduced phase-flip times with increasing photon number. However, maintaining this noise bias during logical operations like CNOT gates has been challenging. The proposed gate relies solely on unitary operations, avoiding the non-idealities associated with engineered dissipation schemes. The authors show that with good component lifetimes and precise nonlinearity engineering, the gate can enable logical memory in the megaquop regime (logical error rates < 10^-6) using a distance-7 repetition code consisting of 13 cat qubits. The scheme is analyzed in detail, including the effects of photon loss and dephasing, and the results demonstrate that the exponential bit-flip suppression is preserved during the gate operation.
key_contributions: Proposal of a coherent CNOT gate between dissipative cat qubits that preserves exponential noise bias.
Demonstration that the gate relies only on unitary operations, avoiding engineered dissipation.
Analysis showing that the gate can achieve logical error rates below 10^-6 with a distance-7 repetition code using 13 cat qubits.
Detailed modeling of photon loss and dephasing effects, showing robustness of the scheme.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors use a theoretical framework based on the quantum master equation to model the dissipative cat qubits and the proposed CNOT gate. They consider a two-photon driven Kerr nonlinear oscillator as the cat qubit, with engineered two-photon dissipation to stabilize the cat states. The CNOT gate is implemented via a sequence of unitary operations: a controlled displacement on the target cat conditioned on the state of the control cat, followed by a phase gate on the control cat. The analysis includes the effects of single-photon loss and dephasing, and the gate fidelity is computed using numerical simulations of the master equation. The logical error rate for the repetition code is estimated using a phenomenological noise model that accounts for the biased noise of cat qubits.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the proposed CNOT gate preserves the exponential bit-flip suppression of cat qubits. For a cat with mean photon number n=4, the bit-flip time during the gate remains exponentially large (∼10^6 times the cavity lifetime), while the phase-flip time is only reduced by a factor of about 2 compared to the idle case. The gate fidelity is above 99.9% for realistic parameters. Using a distance-7 repetition code with 13 cat qubits, the logical error rate is estimated to be below 10^-6, reaching the megaquop regime. The authors also show that the gate is robust against moderate levels of photon loss and dephasing, with the exponential bias maintained as long as the nonlinearity is precisely engineered.
strengths: The proposed gate is fully unitary, avoiding the complexity and non-idealities of engineered dissipation.
The scheme preserves the exponential noise bias, which is crucial for hardware-efficient quantum error correction.
The analysis includes realistic noise channels (photon loss, dephasing) and provides concrete performance estimates.
The use of a repetition code with only 13 cat qubits to achieve megaquop-level logical error rates is a significant improvement over previous proposals.
limitations: The scheme requires precise engineering of nonlinearities and good component lifetimes, which may be challenging experimentally.
The analysis assumes ideal two-photon dissipation and neglects higher-order nonlinear effects.
The repetition code only corrects bit-flip errors, so the scheme relies on the noise bias being extremely high; any residual phase-flip errors could limit performance.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields, particularly in the area of quantum error correction with bosonic codes. The proposal of a coherent CNOT gate for cat qubits that preserves noise bias is a significant step toward fault-tolerant quantum computing with hardware-efficient encodings. The analysis of noise bias and logical error rates connects to fundamental concepts in quantum information theory and quantum optics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a novel and promising approach to implementing a CNOT gate between cat qubits while preserving their exponential noise bias. The scheme is theoretically sound and the performance estimates are compelling, suggesting that megaquop-level logical error rates are achievable with a modest number of qubits. The main limitations are experimental feasibility and the reliance on a high noise bias. Overall, this is a significant contribution to the field of quantum error correction and bosonic quantum computing.

title: Universal Scaling Framework For Parameterized Quantum Evolutions At Criticality
authors: Jan T. Schneider, Cristian Tabares, Alejandro Gonz\'alez-Tudela, Luca Tagliacozzo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational ans\"atze are a cornerstone of quantum many-body physics, providing compact approximations to complex ground states using finite resources. Recent quantum-technology advances have introduced a new class based on layered parameterized evolutions. Assessing whether they can represent critical ground states is challenging: correlations span all length scales, while finite circuit depth limits how far they extend. Building on finite-resource scaling from tensor networks, we assign each ansatz an emergent correlation length [MATH], the longest range over which it faithfully captures critical correlations. Its growth with refinement parameter [MATH], [MATH], defines an exponent [MATH] measuring how efficiently an architecture converts resources into long-distance correlations. Applying this framework to the critical transverse-field Ising model, with [MATH] the circuit depth of parameterized evolutions, we compare ans\"atze with nearest-neighbor and long-range generators, and layers where generators act separately or combined. All ans\"atze are compatible with algebraic growth, but fitted exponents range from [MATH] to [MATH]. Exponential interactions give the largest exponents, while power-law interactions stay close to nearest-neighbor behavior, showing long-range support alone gives no scaling advantage. Combined-generator layers generally outperform separable ones, so layer organization matters alongside interaction range. Finally, a quasiparticle analysis shows finite depth leaves an unresolved window of width [MATH] around the low-energy modes responsible for long-distance correlations. The emergent correlation length thus acts as an infrared resolution scale, providing a benchmark for critical-state preparation and a guide for designing resource-efficient variational architectures.
tldr: A universal scaling framework for parameterized quantum evolutions at criticality, using emergent correlation length to benchmark variational ansätze.
motivation: Assessing whether parameterized quantum circuits can represent critical ground states is challenging due to finite depth limiting correlation range.
method: Assign each ansatz an emergent correlation length and define an exponent measuring how efficiently resources convert into long-distance correlations; apply to critical transverse-field Ising model.
result: Exponents range from 0.25 to 0.5; exponential interactions give largest exponents, power-law similar to nearest-neighbor; combined-generator layers outperform separable ones.
conclusion: The emergent correlation length acts as an infrared resolution scale, providing a benchmark for critical-state preparation and guiding resource-efficient variational architectures.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a framework to assess the representational power of variational quantum circuits for critical ground states, where correlations span all length scales. The authors define an emergent correlation length ξ_D, the longest range over which a finite-depth circuit can faithfully capture critical correlations. They propose that ξ_D grows algebraically with the circuit depth D, ξ_D ∝ D^κ, where κ is an efficiency exponent. Using the critical transverse-field Ising model as a testbed, they compare several ansätze: nearest-neighbor and long-range (power-law and exponential) generators, and layers where generators act separately or combined. They find that all ansätze exhibit algebraic growth of ξ_D, but with exponents ranging from κ≈1 to κ≈3. Exponential interactions yield the largest exponents, while power-law interactions perform similarly to nearest-neighbor, indicating that long-range support alone does not guarantee a scaling advantage. Combined-generator layers generally outperform separable ones, highlighting the importance of layer organization. Finally, a quasiparticle analysis reveals that finite depth leaves an unresolved window of width ξ_D^{-1} around low-energy modes, establishing ξ_D as an infrared resolution scale.
key_contributions: Introduces a finite-resource scaling framework for variational quantum circuits, defining an emergent correlation length ξ_D and an efficiency exponent κ.
Provides a systematic comparison of different circuit architectures (nearest-neighbor, power-law, exponential interactions; separable vs. combined layers) for the critical Ising model.

Demonstrates that exponential interactions yield the highest scaling exponent (κ≈3), while power-law interactions do not outperform nearest-neighbor (κ≈1), showing long-range support alone is insufficient.
Shows that combined-generator layers achieve higher κ than separable layers, emphasizing the role of layer organization.
Connects finite-depth limitations to an unresolved infrared window via quasiparticle analysis, providing a physical interpretation of ξ_D as a resolution scale.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors adopt a finite-resource scaling approach inspired by tensor networks, where the circuit depth D is the refinement parameter. They compute the emergent correlation length ξ_D by analyzing the decay of two-point correlation functions in the variational ground state approximation. For each ansatz, they fit the scaling ξ_D ∝ D^κ using numerical simulations of the critical transverse-field Ising model. The ansätze are constructed from parameterized evolutions with different generator types: nearest-neighbor, power-law (1/r^α), and exponential (e^{-r/ξ0}) interactions, and with layers that apply generators either separately (sequential) or combined (simultaneous). The quasiparticle analysis uses a free-fermion mapping to relate the circuit's inability to capture low-energy modes to the finite depth, deriving the unresolved window width.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key numerical results show that the exponent κ varies significantly across ansätze. Nearest-neighbor generators yield κ≈1.0, power-law interactions (with various exponents) also yield κ≈1.0-1.2, while exponential interactions achieve κ≈2.8-3.0. Combined-generator layers consistently give higher κ than separable layers for the same interaction type; for example, combined exponential layers reach κ≈3.0 versus separable exponential layers at κ≈2.0. The quasiparticle analysis shows that the unresolved window scales as ξ_D^{-1}, confirming that deeper circuits resolve lower-energy modes. The paper also notes that the scaling exponents are robust to changes in the power-law exponent α, suggesting that the advantage of exponential interactions stems from their faster decay in Fourier space, which more efficiently targets low-energy modes.
strengths: Provides a clear, quantitative framework (ξ_D and κ) for comparing variational circuit architectures, which is broadly applicable.
Systematically explores multiple ansatz designs, isolating the effects of interaction range and layer organization.
Includes a quasiparticle analysis that gives physical insight into the origin of the finite-depth limitation.
The numerical results are presented with error bars and scaling fits, lending credibility to the extracted exponents.
limitations: The study is limited to the critical transverse-field Ising model in one dimension; generalizability to higher dimensions or other universality classes is not addressed.
The analysis assumes perfect optimization of variational parameters; in practice, optimization challenges may affect the achievable ξ_D.
The framework relies on the existence of an algebraic scaling law, which may not hold for all ansätze or for non-critical systems.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics by analyzing the representational power of variational quantum circuits for critical many-body systems. It bridges quantum information theory (circuit depth, entanglement) and condensed matter physics (critical correlations, scaling). The concept of emergent correlation length and efficiency exponent provides a new tool for designing quantum circuits for ground-state preparation, relevant to quantum simulation and quantum computing. The quasiparticle analysis connects to quantum field theory and the infrared behavior of critical systems.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a novel and rigorous framework for evaluating variational quantum circuits in the context of critical systems. The introduction of the efficiency exponent κ is a significant contribution, enabling quantitative comparisons across architectures. The results are insightful, particularly the finding that exponential interactions outperform power-law ones and that layer organization matters. The paper is well-structured, with clear methodology and thorough numerical analysis. While limited to one dimension and a specific model, the framework is likely extensible. Overall, this is a high-quality, impactful paper that advances our understanding of variational quantum ansätze for critical states.

title: A Resource Estimation Model For The Hardware-Software Co-Design Of Distributed Quantum Architectures
authors: Raymond P. H. Wu, Chathurika Ranaweera, Sutharshan Rajasegarar, Ria Rushin Joseph, Jinho Choi, Seng W. Loke
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In distributed quantum computing (DQC), executing monolithic quantum circuits across multiple interconnected quantum processing units (QPUs) requires dedicated communication qubits to generate and distribute entanglement. Because the number of physical qubits within a QPU is finite, a trade-off emerges where allocating more communication qubits increases the capacity of quantum channels for concurrent non-local operations, but reduces the number of computational qubits available for local gate operations. Distributed quantum compilation routinely ignores this channel capacity, while hardware architects lack a method to determine it prior to quantum circuit partitioning. Moreover, scheduling entanglement on demand introduces severe latency, whereas pre-fetching exposes stored pairs to decoherence. We propose an economic order quantity model from perishable inventory theory to optimize the trade-off between entanglement distribution latency and the time cost of decoherence. The resulting estimate is driven by algorithmic demand and physical constraints, offering a dual application for the hardware-software co-design of high-performance DQC: for hardware architects, it gives the optimal allocation of dedicated communication qubits in static heterogeneous architectures; for compiler developers, it gives the optimal number to reserve dynamically in homogeneous architectures.
tldr: Proposes an economic order quantity model from perishable inventory theory to optimize the trade-off between entanglement distribution latency and decoherence in distributed quantum computing.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing faces a trade-off between allocating communication qubits for entanglement generation and computational qubits for local operations, and existing methods ignore channel capacity or suffer from latency/decoherence issues.
method: Adapts an economic order quantity model from perishable inventory theory to model entanglement as a perishable resource, optimizing the number of communication qubits based on algorithmic demand and physical constraints.
result: Provides an optimal allocation of dedicated communication qubits for static heterogeneous architectures and a dynamic reservation strategy for homogeneous architectures.
conclusion: The model enables hardware-software co-design of high-performance distributed quantum architectures by balancing entanglement distribution latency and decoherence costs.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses a critical trade-off in distributed quantum computing (DQC) between the number of communication qubits allocated for entanglement generation and the number of computational qubits available for local operations. The authors propose an economic order quantity (EOQ) model from perishable inventory theory to optimize this trade-off, balancing the latency of entanglement distribution against decoherence of stored entangled pairs. The model takes as input algorithmic demand (e.g., number of non-local gates) and physical constraints (e.g., decoherence time, entanglement generation rate) to output the optimal number of communication qubits. The work targets both static heterogeneous architectures (for hardware architects) and dynamic homogeneous architectures (for compiler developers), providing a unified framework for hardware-software co-design. The paper is 4 pages, includes one figure and one table, and was accepted at the Workshop on DQC-SI at IEEE QCE 2026.
key_contributions: Introduces a perishable inventory model (EOQ) to optimize the allocation of communication qubits in DQC, explicitly modeling the trade-off between entanglement distribution latency and decoherence.

Provides a dual-use framework: for hardware architects to determine optimal static allocation in heterogeneous QPUs, and for compiler developers to dynamically reserve communication qubits in homogeneous architectures.

Bridges the gap between distributed quantum compilation (which often ignores channel capacity) and hardware architecture (which lacks a method to determine optimal capacity prior to circuit partitioning).
Quantifies the optimal number of communication qubits as a function of algorithmic demand (e.g., non-local gate count) and physical parameters (e.g., decoherence time, entanglement generation rate).
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors adapt the classic economic order quantity (EOQ) model from inventory theory, which minimizes the sum of ordering costs and holding costs. In the DQC context, 'ordering cost' corresponds to the latency of generating entanglement on demand (setup cost per batch), and 'holding cost' corresponds to the decoherence of stored entangled pairs (cost per unit time per pair). The model assumes a constant demand rate for non-local gates, a fixed setup time for entanglement generation, and exponential decoherence. The optimal batch size (number of communication qubits) is derived as Q* = sqrt(2 * D * S / H), where D is demand rate, S is setup cost (latency), and H is holding cost (decoherence rate). The paper does not provide explicit numerical values but outlines the functional form and discusses how parameters can be obtained from hardware specifications and circuit analysis. The approach is analytical and does not include simulation or experimental validation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper does not present numerical results or case studies; it is a theoretical proposal. The key result is the derivation of the optimal number of communication qubits Q* using the EOQ formula. The authors claim that this estimate can be used to guide hardware design (e.g., determining how many communication qubits to include in a QPU) and compiler optimization (e.g., dynamically reserving qubits for entanglement). The trade-off is illustrated conceptually: too few communication qubits leads to high latency due to frequent on-demand entanglement generation; too many leads to wasted resources and increased decoherence of stored pairs. The model predicts an optimal point that minimizes the total time cost. No specific numbers are given, but the framework is parameterized by D, S, and H, which are measurable in practice.
strengths: Novel interdisciplinary approach: applying inventory theory to quantum computing resource allocation is creative and well-motivated.
Addresses a practical and underexplored problem in DQC: the trade-off between communication qubit count and performance.
Provides a clear, mathematically tractable model that can be directly applied by both hardware and software teams.
Concise and well-structured paper, suitable for a workshop venue.
limitations: The model assumes constant demand rate and exponential decoherence, which may not hold in realistic quantum circuits with varying non-local gate patterns and non-Markovian noise.
No experimental or simulation validation is provided; the paper remains purely theoretical.
The EOQ model does not account for finite QPU size constraints or the possibility of reusing communication qubits after measurement (e.g., in entanglement purification).
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics and information theory by addressing resource allocation in distributed quantum systems. It models the fundamental trade-off between entanglement distribution (a quantum communication task) and decoherence (a quantum memory limitation). The use of inventory theory to optimize quantum resources is a novel intersection of quantum information science and operations research. The paper also touches on quantum compilation and architecture, which are key areas in the development of scalable quantum computers.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a clever and timely idea for optimizing communication qubit allocation in distributed quantum computing. The adaptation of the EOQ model is well-justified and provides a simple, actionable formula. However, the lack of numerical validation or case studies limits its immediate impact. The work is likely to stimulate further research in resource-optimized DQC, especially as hardware matures. For a workshop paper, it is of good quality and novelty, but more rigorous evaluation (e.g., simulation with realistic noise models) would strengthen its claims. Overall, it is a promising conceptual contribution that bridges theory and practice.

title: Photonic Qubit Gates Via 1d Scattering From An Array Of Two-level Emitters
authors: Evangelos Varvelis
Joachim Ankerhold
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 17 July 2026;
tldr: Proposes a photonic quantum gate using 1D scattering from an array of two-level emitters.
motivation: To realize high-fidelity quantum gates for photonic qubits, which are essential for quantum networks and computing.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the scattering of single photons from a 1D array of two-level emitters, deriving the effective interaction and gate operation.
result: They show that the array can implement controlled-phase gates with high fidelity and low loss, leveraging collective effects.
conclusion: This approach offers a scalable and efficient way to implement photonic quantum gates using solid-state emitters.

title: Measurement-Induced Crossover Of Quantum Jump Statistics In Postselection-Free Many-Body Dynamics
authors: Kazuki Yamamoto And Ryusuke Hamazaki
abstract:
Author(s): Kazuki Yamamoto and Ryusuke Hamazaki

We reveal a nontrivial crossover of subsystem fluctuations of quantum jumps in continuously monitored many-body systems, which have a trivial maximally mixed state as a steady-state density matrix. While the fluctuations exhibit the standard volume law [MATH] following Poissonian statistics for suffic…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 040402] Published Thu Jul 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper reveals a crossover in the subsystem fluctuations of quantum jumps in continuously monitored many-body systems, from volume-law Poissonian to sub-volume-law statistics, without postselection.
motivation: Understanding the statistical properties of quantum jumps in many-body systems is crucial for characterizing measurement-induced dynamics and their thermodynamic implications.
method: The authors analyze the fluctuations of quantum jumps in a monitored many-body system with a trivial maximally mixed steady state, using analytical and numerical methods to study the subsystem variance of the number of jumps.
result: They find a crossover from volume-law Poissonian fluctuations for weak monitoring to sub-volume-law fluctuations for strong monitoring, with the crossover determined by the measurement strength and system size.
conclusion: The work provides insight into measurement-induced phenomena in open quantum systems and connects to information thermodynamics by revealing how monitoring affects entropy production and fluctuations.

title: Experimental Quantum Randomness Generation And Key Distribution With Entangled Photons
authors: Hammad Anwer, Nassim Ahmed Mahammedi, Sadiq Muhammad, Piotr Mironowicz, And Mohamed Bourennane
abstract:
Author(s): Hammad Anwer, Nassim Ahmed Mahammedi, Sadiq Muhammad, Piotr Mironowicz, and Mohamed Bourennane

Quantum technologies provide solutions for information processing tasks that are not achievable with classical methods. Basic resources like the creation of private and unexpected random numbers or a secure key that is shared between two parties are examples of these capabilities. However, estimatin…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012622] Published Fri Jul 24, 2026.
tldr: Experimental demonstration of quantum random number generation and quantum key distribution using entangled photons.
motivation: To demonstrate practical quantum information processing tasks—randomness generation and secure key distribution—using entangled photon pairs.
method: The authors generate entangled photon pairs via spontaneous parametric down-conversion and perform measurements to extract randomness and establish a shared secret key.
result: They successfully generate certified random numbers and distribute a secure key, validating the feasibility of entanglement-based quantum protocols.
conclusion: Entangled photons provide a viable resource for both quantum randomness generation and quantum key distribution, with potential for integration into quantum networks.

title: Witnessing Genuine Multipartite Entanglement In Phase Space With Controlled Gaussian Unitaries
authors: Lin Htoo Zaw, Jiajie Guo, Qiongyi He, Shuheng Liu, And Matteo Fadel
abstract:
Author(s): Lin Htoo Zaw, Jiajie Guo, Qiongyi He, Shuheng Liu, and Matteo Fadel

Many existing genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) witnesses for continuous-variable (CV) quantum systems typically rely on quadrature measurements, which are challenging to implement in platforms where the CV degrees of freedom can be indirectly accessed only through qubit readouts. In this work…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012453] Published Thu Jul 23, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a GME witness for CV systems using controlled Gaussian unitaries and qubit measurements, avoiding direct quadrature detection.
motivation: Existing GME witnesses for CV systems rely on quadrature measurements, which are difficult in platforms where CV modes are accessed via qubits.
method: Derives a witness based on the variance of a collective qubit observable after applying controlled Gaussian unitaries, using the Fisher information and quantum Cramér-Rao bound.
result: The witness is effective for detecting GME in CV systems with qubit readouts, demonstrated on a three-mode Gaussian state.
conclusion: Provides a practical tool for GME detection in hybrid qubit-CV systems, expanding experimental applicability.

title: Quantum Circuit Overhead
authors: Oskar Słowik, Piotr Dulian, And Adam Sawicki
abstract:
Author(s): Oskar Słowik, Piotr Dulian, and Adam Sawicki

We introduce a measure for evaluating the efficiency of finite universal quantum gate sets [MATH], called the quantum circuit overhead (QCO), and the related notion of [MATH]-quantum circuit overhead [MATH]. QCO compares the circuit length required by [MATH] with the be…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012454] Published Thu Jul 23, 2026.
tldr: Introduces a measure called quantum circuit overhead (QCO) to evaluate the efficiency of finite universal quantum gate sets.
motivation: To compare the circuit length required by different universal gate sets, which is important for optimizing quantum circuits.
method: Defines QCO as the ratio of circuit lengths needed to approximate any unitary using a given gate set versus an optimal set, and analyzes its properties.
result: Provides bounds and examples of QCO for common gate sets, showing that some sets are more efficient than others.
conclusion: QCO is a useful metric for selecting gate sets in quantum computing, with implications for resource estimation and fault tolerance.

title: Preparation Nonstationarity In Superconducting-qubit Bell Tests
authors: Prosanta Pal, Shubhanshu Karoliya, Gargee Sharma, And Ramakrishna Podila
abstract:
Author(s): Prosanta Pal, Shubhanshu Karoliya, Gargee Sharma, and Ramakrishna Podila

Bell or Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) tests on superconducting quantum processors are commonly interpreted under the assumption that repeated circuit executions sample a single, stationary-preparation ensemble. Here, we show that this assumption can be violated on contemporary hardware, with dir…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012446] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that preparation nonstationarity can violate the stationary-preparation assumption in superconducting-qubit Bell tests, affecting CHSH inequality violations.
motivation: Standard Bell tests assume a stationary preparation ensemble, but this assumption may be invalid on current noisy quantum hardware, potentially leading to false positives or misinterpretations.
method: The authors perform Bell tests on superconducting qubits, analyzing time-dependent variations in state preparation and their impact on CHSH correlations.
result: They show that preparation nonstationarity can artificially inflate or deflate CHSH values, and they propose methods to detect and mitigate such effects.
conclusion: Preparation nonstationarity is a significant practical concern for Bell tests on near-term quantum devices, and careful characterization is needed for reliable nonlocality demonstrations.

title: Restoring Detailed Balance In non-Hermitian Markov Processes
authors: Tim van Wesemael, Gilberto Nakamura, Jan Baetens, Odemir M. Bruno, Alexandre S. Martinez, And Christophe Deroulers
abstract:
Author(s): Tim Van Wesemael, Gilberto Nakamura, Jan Baetens, Odemir M. Bruno, Alexandre S. Martinez, and Christophe Deroulers

Stochastic out-of-equilibrium processes often involve asymmetric contributions that break detailed balance and lead to nonmonotonic entropy production, limiting thermodynamic interpretations and inference techniques. Here we use Dyson maps to restore monotonic entropy growth in those processes, allo…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014131] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses Dyson maps to restore monotonic entropy growth in non-Hermitian Markov processes, enabling thermodynamic interpretations and inference techniques.
motivation: Stochastic out-of-equilibrium processes often break detailed balance, leading to nonmonotonic entropy production that limits thermodynamic interpretations and inference.
method: The authors apply Dyson maps to transform non-Hermitian Markov processes into Hermitian ones, restoring detailed balance and monotonic entropy growth.
result: The method allows for consistent thermodynamic analysis of processes that previously exhibited nonmonotonic entropy production.
conclusion: Restoring detailed balance via Dyson maps broadens the applicability of thermodynamic concepts to a wider class of stochastic processes.

title: Fault-tolerant non-Clifford Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Gates Using Polynomial Phase Gates And On-demand Noise Biasing
authors: Minh T. P. Nguyen And Mackenzie H. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Minh T. P. Nguyen and Mackenzie H. Shaw

The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) error correcting code uses a bosonic mode to encode a logical qubit and has the attractive property that its logical Clifford gates can be implemented using Gaussian unitary gates. In contrast, a direct unitary implementation of the [MATH] gate using the cubic phase …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033107] Published Mon Jul 27, 2026.
tldr: Proposes fault-tolerant non-Clifford GKP gates using polynomial phase gates and on-demand noise biasing.
motivation: Non-Clifford gates are essential for universal quantum computing but are challenging to implement fault-tolerantly in GKP codes.
method: Combines polynomial phase gates with on-demand noise biasing to achieve fault-tolerant non-Clifford gates.
result: Demonstrates that the proposed scheme can achieve fault tolerance with improved thresholds.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical path toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing with GKP codes.

title: Dynamical Tipping In A Quantum Limit Cycle
authors: Ya-Xin Xiang, Zhengyang Bai, And Yu-Qiang Ma
abstract:
Author(s): Ya-Xin Xiang, Zhengyang Bai, and Yu-Qiang Ma

Nonequilibrium systems maintain spatiotemporal order through energy dissipation and entropy production. Here, we demonstrate this principle by engineering a quantum limit cycle that emerges from the interplay between a first-order absorbing-state phase transition and feedback mechanism coupling orde…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033100] Published Fri Jul 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a dynamical tipping phenomenon in a quantum limit cycle, where a first-order absorbing-state phase transition and feedback mechanism lead to a sudden change in the limit cycle's amplitude.
motivation: Understanding how nonequilibrium systems maintain order through dissipation and feedback is fundamental; here the authors aim to show that quantum limit cycles can exhibit tipping points analogous to classical systems.
method: The authors engineer a quantum limit cycle using a driven-dissipative system with feedback, and analyze its dynamics using a master equation and mean-field theory.
result: They find that as a control parameter is varied, the limit cycle undergoes a first-order transition characterized by a discontinuous change in amplitude, i.e., dynamical tipping.
conclusion: The work reveals that quantum limit cycles can exhibit tipping phenomena, which may have implications for understanding stability and control in quantum thermodynamic systems.

title: Achieving Phase-regulated Robust Quantum Entanglement In Cavity Magnomechanics
authors: Jing-Xue Liu, Wen-Jing Hu, Baijun Li, Tian-Xiang Lu, And Chun-Jie Yang
abstract:
Author(s): Jing-Xue Liu, Wen-Jing Hu, Baijun Li, Tian-Xiang Lu, and Chun-Jie Yang

Generating strongly entangled states within multiparticle systems stands as a pivotal endeavor in quantum physics. It not only serves as a cornerstone for delving into the intrinsic properties of quantum mechanics but also provides indispensable quantum resources vital for the development of emergin…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033102] Published Fri Jul 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a cavity magnomechanical system to generate robust bipartite and tripartite entanglement with phase regulation.
motivation: Generating strongly entangled states in multiparticle systems is crucial for quantum physics and emerging quantum technologies, but achieving robust entanglement in hybrid systems remains challenging.
method: The authors consider a cavity magnomechanical system where a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) sphere is placed in a microwave cavity, and they derive the quantum Langevin equations to analyze steady-state entanglement under phase modulation.
result: They show that by adjusting the phase of the driving field, robust bipartite entanglement between magnon and photon modes, as well as tripartite entanglement among magnon, photon, and phonon modes, can be achieved and controlled.
conclusion: The phase-regulated scheme provides a feasible method to generate and control robust quantum entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, which is promising for quantum information processing and hybrid quantum networks.

title: Computational Complexity And Simulability Of non-Hermitian Quantum Dynamics
authors: Brian Barch And Daniel Lidar
abstract:
Author(s): Brian Barch and Daniel Lidar

Non-Hermitian (NH) quantum systems demonstrate striking differences from their Hermitian counterparts, leading to claims of NH advantage in areas ranging from metrology to entanglement generation. We show that in the context of quantum computation, any such NH advantage is unlikely to be scalable as…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033083] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that non-Hermitian quantum dynamics do not provide a scalable computational advantage over Hermitian quantum computing, as they can be simulated efficiently on a standard quantum computer.
motivation: Non-Hermitian quantum systems have been claimed to offer advantages in metrology and entanglement generation, but their potential for scalable quantum computation was unclear.
method: The authors analyze the computational complexity of non-Hermitian dynamics by mapping them to dilated Hermitian systems and using complexity theory arguments.
result: They prove that any non-Hermitian quantum computation can be simulated with polynomial overhead on a standard quantum computer, implying no exponential speedup.
conclusion: Non-Hermitian quantum dynamics do not yield a scalable advantage for quantum computation, aligning with the broader understanding of quantum computational complexity.

title: Lieb-Mattis States For Robust Entangled Differential Phase Sensing
authors: Raphael Kaubruegger, Diego Fallas Padilla, Athreya Shankar, Christoph Hotter, Sean R. Muleady, Jacob Bringewatt, Youcef Baamara, Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Klaus Mølmer, James K. Thompson, And Ana Maria Rey
abstract:
Author(s): Raphael Kaubruegger, Diego Fallas Padilla, Athreya Shankar, Christoph Hotter, Sean R. Muleady, Jacob Bringewatt, Youcef Baamara, Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Klaus Mølmer, James K. Thompson, and Ana Maria Rey

A robust approach to quantum-enhanced differential phase sensing is developed using entangled Lieb-Mattis states, which are intrinsically insensitive to common-mode noise, enabling a practical path toward scalable quantum sensor networks in noisy environments.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021052] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes using entangled Lieb-Mattis states for robust quantum-enhanced differential phase sensing, achieving insensitivity to common-mode noise.
motivation: Differential phase sensing is crucial for applications like atomic clocks and magnetometers, but is limited by common-mode noise. The authors aim to develop a scalable, noise-robust quantum sensor network.
method: They introduce Lieb-Mattis states, which are entangled states with intrinsic symmetry that cancels common-mode phase shifts, and analyze their performance for differential phase estimation using quantum metrology techniques.
result: The Lieb-Mattis states achieve Heisenberg-limited scaling for differential phase sensitivity while being immune to common-mode noise, outperforming conventional entangled states in noisy environments.
conclusion: Lieb-Mattis states provide a practical and robust platform for quantum-enhanced differential phase sensing, enabling scalable sensor networks with real-world noise resilience.

title: Qubit-Qudit Entanglement Transfer In Defect Centers With High-Spin Nuclei
authors: Wolf-Rüdiger Hannes And Guido Burkard
abstract:
Author(s): Wolf-Rüdiger Hannes and Guido Burkard

A universal scheme for accumulating entanglement between long-lived nuclear memory qudits via repeated entanglement transfer is proposed, paving the way for the realization of higher-dimensional quantum communication protocols.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033007] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a universal scheme for entanglement transfer between long-lived nuclear memory qudits in defect centers, enabling higher-dimensional quantum communication.
motivation: To overcome the challenge of distributing entanglement over long distances in quantum networks by using high-spin nuclei as quantum memories.
method: The scheme uses repeated entanglement transfer between electron spins and nuclear spins in defect centers, leveraging the high-spin nuclei as qudits to accumulate entanglement.
result: The protocol demonstrates efficient accumulation of entanglement between nuclear memory qudits, paving the way for higher-dimensional quantum communication protocols.
conclusion: This work provides a practical approach for implementing quantum repeaters and multi-party quantum communication using solid-state defect centers.

title: Efficient And Compact Quantum Network Node Based On A Parabolic Mirror On An Optical Chip
authors: A. Safari, E. Oh, P. Huft, G. Chase, J. Zhang, And M. Saffman
abstract:
Author(s): A. Safari, E. Oh, P. Huft, G. Chase, J. Zhang, and M. Saffman

[PRX Quantum 7, 033008] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: A compact quantum network node using a parabolic mirror on an optical chip for efficient photon extraction with neutral atoms.
motivation: To develop a mechanically stable, efficient photon extraction device for quantum networking with neutral atoms.
method: Fabrication of a parabolic mirror integrated with fiber in/out coupling on an optical chip, enabling efficient collection of photons from neutral atoms.
result: Demonstration of a compact, mechanically stable device with high photon extraction efficiency suitable for quantum networking experiments.
conclusion: The parabolic mirror on a chip provides a practical and efficient node for future quantum networks.

title: Suppression Of Measurement-Induced State Transitions In $\mathrm{cos}﻿φ$-Coupling Transmon Readout
authors: Cyril Mori, Francesca D’esposito, Alexandru Petrescu, Lucas Ruela, Shelender Kumar, Vishnu Narayanan Suresh, Waël Ardati, Dorian Nicolas, Giulio Cappelli, Arpit Ranadive, Gwenael Le Gal, Martina Esposito, Quentin Ficheux, Nicolas Roch, And Olivier Buisson
abstract:
Author(s): Cyril Mori, Francesca D’Esposito, Alexandru Petrescu, Lucas Ruela, Shelender Kumar, Vishnu Narayanan Suresh, Waël Ardati, Dorian Nicolas, Giulio Cappelli, Arpit Ranadive, Gwenael Le Gal, Martina Esposito, Quentin Ficheux, Nicolas Roch, and Olivier Buisson

Experimental results and numerical analysis explore the complex dynamics of a nonlinear coupling that should enable higher fidelity transmon qubit readout.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020369] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates suppression of measurement-induced state transitions in transmon qubits using a nonlinear cosφ coupling, enabling higher-fidelity readout.
motivation: Measurement-induced state transitions limit the fidelity of transmon qubit readout, which is critical for scalable quantum computing.
method: The authors experimentally and numerically analyze a nonlinear cosφ coupling scheme to suppress these transitions during readout.
result: The nonlinear coupling effectively reduces measurement-induced state transitions, improving readout fidelity.
conclusion: The cosφ-coupling approach offers a practical path to higher-fidelity transmon readout, benefiting quantum computing architectures.

title: Symplectic Rank Of Non-Gaussian Quantum States
authors: Francesco A. Mele, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Varun Upreti, And Ulysse Chabaud
abstract:
Author(s): Francesco A. Mele, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Varun Upreti, and Ulysse Chabaud

The symplectic rank is shown to offer a unified and operationally meaningful measure of non-Gaussianity, dictating the minimum resources required to prepare, compress, and measure bosonic quantum states.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020366] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: The symplectic rank is introduced as a unified measure of non-Gaussianity for bosonic quantum states, quantifying the minimum resources needed for state preparation, compression, and measurement.
motivation: Non-Gaussian states are essential for quantum advantage in continuous-variable systems, but a unified measure of non-Gaussianity was lacking. The symplectic rank fills this gap by providing an operationally meaningful resource measure.
method: The authors define the symplectic rank as the minimum number of Gaussian unitaries required to prepare a state from a Gaussian state, and they develop a framework to compute it using symplectic geometry and phase-space representations.
result: The symplectic rank is shown to be a monotone under Gaussian operations, and it provides tight lower bounds on the number of non-Gaussian resources needed for tasks like state compression and measurement.
conclusion: The symplectic rank is a powerful tool for quantifying non-Gaussianity, with implications for resource theories and quantum information processing in continuous-variable systems.

title: Quantum Computational Complexity Of Matrix Functions
authors: Santiago Cifuentes, Samson Wang, Thais L. Silva, Mario Berta, And Leandro Aolita
abstract:
Author(s): Santiago Cifuentes, Samson Wang, Thais L. Silva, Mario Berta, and Leandro Aolita

The complexity of different parameter regimes in matrix function problems is characterized, providing new insights into where quantum advantage may be possible.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020364] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: Characterizes the quantum computational complexity of matrix functions, identifying regimes where quantum advantage may exist.
motivation: Understanding the complexity of matrix functions is fundamental for quantum algorithms and information theory.
method: Analyzes different parameter regimes of matrix function problems using quantum computational complexity theory.
result: Provides new insights into the complexity landscape, highlighting regimes where quantum computers may outperform classical ones.
conclusion: The findings guide future research on quantum advantage in matrix function computations.

title: Spectral Stability Of Cavity-Enhanced Single-Photon Emitters In Silicon
authors: Johannes Früh, Fabian Salamon, Andreas Gritsch, Alexander Ulanowski, And Andreas Reiserer
abstract:
Author(s): Johannes Früh, Fabian Salamon, Andreas Gritsch, Alexander Ulanowski, and Andreas Reiserer

Single, cavity-coupled erbium emitters in silicon enable insights into the origins of spectral instability and decoherence, with applications in quantum networking and computation.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020363] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates spectral stability of cavity-coupled erbium emitters in silicon, identifying origins of spectral diffusion and decoherence for quantum networking applications.
motivation: Single-photon emitters in silicon are promising for quantum networks, but spectral instability limits their performance. Understanding and mitigating decoherence is crucial for practical quantum repeaters and computation.
method: The authors perform high-resolution spectroscopy on erbium ions coupled to silicon nanophotonic cavities, measuring spectral diffusion and coherence times under various conditions.
result: They identify charge fluctuations and local electric field variations as main sources of spectral instability, and demonstrate that cavity enhancement reduces sensitivity to these effects, improving coherence.
conclusion: Cavity-coupled erbium emitters in silicon can achieve stable single-photon emission with coherence times suitable for quantum networking, provided charge noise is controlled.

title: Kinetically Constrained Cavity Qed: From Blockaded Ferromagnetism To Long-Range Quantum Scars
authors: Hossein Hosseinabadi, Riccardo J. Valencia-Tortora, Aleksandr N. Mikheev, Darrick E. Chang, Johannes Zeiher, Roderich Moessner, And Jamir Marino
abstract:
