title: Machine Learning Of Quantum Entanglement From Noisy Measurements
authors: Artur Czerwinski, Maciej Wi\'sniewski, Pawe{\l} Moszczy\'nski
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we investigate the application of Machine Learning (ML) algorithms to the identification and quantitative characterization of quantum entanglement in polarization-entangled photon pairs. The analysis is based on simulated symmetric, informationally complete, positive operator-valued measure (SIC-POVM) measurement data, where each two-qubit state is represented by a 16-dimensional measurement vector corresponding to experimentally accessible coincidence counts. The generated SIC-POVM measurement data include Poissonian shot noise. Several supervised ML algorithms, including Logistic Regression, k-Nearest Neighbors, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines, and Random Forests, are applied to the classification of separable and entangled states directly from raw measurement data, without explicit density matrix reconstruction or the use of conventional separability criteria. The study additionally explores clustering methods and nonlinear regression techniques for estimating continuous entanglement measures. The obtained results demonstrate that ML methods can achieve very high classification accuracy, even under extremely limited training conditions. These findings indicate that ML may provide an efficient alternative to conventional quantum-state analysis under simulated Poissonian noise conditions.
tldr: This paper applies machine learning to classify and quantify entanglement from noisy SIC-POVM measurements without state reconstruction.
motivation: Efficient entanglement detection from raw measurement data is desirable, especially under noise, to avoid full tomography.
method: Supervised ML algorithms (Logistic Regression, k-NN, Decision Trees, SVM, Random Forests) are trained on simulated SIC-POVM data with Poissonian noise to classify separable vs. entangled states and estimate entanglement measures.
result: ML methods achieve high classification accuracy even with limited training data, demonstrating robustness to noise.
conclusion: Machine learning offers an efficient alternative to conventional quantum state analysis for entanglement characterization under realistic noise conditions.

title: Response Morphologies Of A Canonical Fluctuation Diagnostic Across Ehrenfest Phase Transitions
authors: Fangfang Wang, Wei Liu, Ying Tang, Zengru Di
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microcanonical inflection-point analysis identifies MIPA-type higher-order transition structures from derivatives of the microcanonical entropy. Until recently, however, there was no canonical formulation for probing the corresponding fluctuation-level behavior directly from measurable energy fluctuations without reconstructing the density of states. Previous work addressed this limitation by introducing a canonical fluctuation diagnostic that quantifies energy-fluctuation asymmetry. Here, we investigate how this diagnostic behaves across representative first-, second-, and third-order phase transitions in the Ehrenfest classification. We consider the eight-state Potts model, the two-dimensional Ising model, and ideal three-dimensional Bose--Einstein condensation. The Potts and Ising systems exhibit a robust paired-extremum structure of the diagnostic near their respective transition regions, whereas ideal Bose--Einstein condensation exhibits a discontinuous response at the condensation temperature in the thermodynamic limit. These results show that a single fluctuation-based observable can display qualitatively distinct response morphologies across thermodynamic regimes, reflecting sensitivity to the nature of the underlying phase transition rather than serving as a direct classifier of Ehrenfest order.
tldr: This paper studies a canonical fluctuation diagnostic across first-, second-, and third-order phase transitions, revealing distinct response morphologies.
motivation: To understand how energy-fluctuation asymmetry behaves across different types of phase transitions without reconstructing the density of states.
method: The authors analyze the fluctuation diagnostic in the eight-state Potts model, 2D Ising model, and ideal Bose-Einstein condensation, comparing its behavior near transition points.
result: The Potts and Ising models show a paired-extremum structure, while Bose-Einstein condensation exhibits a discontinuous response at the condensation temperature.
conclusion: The fluctuation diagnostic is sensitive to the nature of the phase transition but does not directly classify Ehrenfest order.

The Potts and Ising models exhibit a robust paired-extremum structure near their transition regions, while Bose-Einstein condensation shows a discontinuous response at the condensation temperature in the thermodynamic limit. title: Revisiting The Invariant Ring Of Two-qubit Mixed States
authors: Lin Zhang Bing Xie
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local unitary equivalence serves as the cornerstone for classifying entanglement in bipartite quantum systems. Mathematically, it reduces to the study of polynomial invariants of the density matrix under the action of local unitary groups. The collection of all such polynomial invariants forms a ring, known as the invariant ring. However, identifying the complete generators of the invariant ring is the central issue. In 2007, for the two-qubit system, King et al fully characterized the structure of the invariant ring and determined its Cohen--Macaulay decomposition. In this paper, we revisit their work, with a focus on the computation of the Molien series and the construction of invariants. On one hand, we rigorously derive the Molien series via explicit contour integration over the maximal torus, filling in all previously omitted computational steps. On the other hand, we systematically construct all invariants using a graphical method, and then reduce the candidate set by applying various identities and algebraic relations, obtaining a generating set consisting of 21 invariants. This paper aims to make this important result more widely accessible to researchers in quantum information and invariant theory through the above discussions.

motivation: Local unitary equivalence is key to classifying entanglement in bipartite systems, and the full characterization of the invariant ring for two-qubit states was previously incomplete in terms of explicit computational steps.
method: The authors compute the Molien series via explicit contour integration over the maximal torus and construct invariants using a graphical method, then reduce the candidate set using algebraic identities.
result: A generating set of 21 polynomial invariants for the two-qubit mixed state invariant ring is obtained, with all computational steps made explicit.
conclusion: The work makes the structure of the invariant ring more accessible to researchers in quantum information and invariant theory, but does not present novel physical insights or applications.

The result characterizes the decomposition rather than the divergence, and is therefore complementary to the axiomatic characterizations of relative entropy due to Shore-Johnson, Csisz\'ar and Amari, which it neither uses nor extends.
tldr: This paper proves a uniqueness theorem characterizing the variational free energy decomposition, showing that only the Gibbs-Bogoliubov identity (relative entropy) admits an exact additive decomposition under mild conditions.
motivation: Variational free energy decompositions are central to mean-field theory and Bayesian inference, but it was unclear which functionals beyond relative entropy satisfy such exact identities.
method: The author reduces the hypotheses to a homomorphism from the multiplicative group of positive functions into ℝ and uses the second-order vanishing of relative entropy at its minimum to prove uniqueness.
result: The only functional satisfying the given conditions (additive separability, nonnegativity, vanishing at equality) is the relative entropy, and the decomposition is the Gibbs-Bogoliubov identity.
conclusion: The result characterizes the decomposition rather than the divergence, complementing axiomatic characterizations of relative entropy without extending them.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper investigates variational free energy and its exact decomposition into a functional and a divergence term. For a finite system with reference measure p and weight ℓ, the variational free energy F(Q;p,ℓ)=D(Q∥p)−E_Q[logℓ] satisfies the identity logZ(p,ℓ)=−F(Q;p,ℓ)+D(Q∥π), where Z is the partition function and π the Gibbs measure. This identity is central to mean-field theory and Bayesian variational inference. The authors ask which functionals G and Δ admit a similar exact decomposition logZ=−G+Δ, with Δ depending only on Q and π, G additively separable in reference and weight, and Δ nonnegative and zero only at Q=π. They prove that under these conditions, G must equal F and Δ must equal the relative entropy D(Q∥π). The proof reduces the hypotheses to a homomorphism from the multiplicative group of positive functions to (ℝ,+) and uses the second-order vanishing of relative entropy at its minimum. Counterexamples show each hypothesis is necessary. The result characterizes the decomposition rather than the divergence itself, complementing axiomatic characterizations of relative entropy by Shore-Johnson, Csiszár, and Amari.
key_contributions: Proves a uniqueness theorem for the exact decomposition of logZ into a separable functional and a nonnegative divergence that vanishes only at the Gibbs measure.
Identifies the necessary and sufficient conditions under which the decomposition must be the Gibbs-Bogoliubov form: G=F and Δ=D(Q∥π).
Provides counterexamples demonstrating that each hypothesis (additive separability, nonnegativity, zero-minimum) is necessary.
Shows that the result is complementary to existing axiomatic characterizations of relative entropy, as it characterizes the decomposition rather than the divergence itself.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper uses a functional analytic and information-theoretic approach. The authors assume a finite system with a reference measure p and a positive weight ℓ, and consider functionals G and Δ that satisfy logZ=−G+Δ. They impose three key hypotheses: (i) G is additively separable into a term depending on the reference measure and a term depending on the weight, with mild regularity; (ii) Δ is a function of Q and π only; (iii) Δ is nonnegative and vanishes precisely at Q=π. The proof proceeds by reducing these hypotheses to a homomorphism from the multiplicative group of positive functions to (ℝ,+). Using the fact that relative entropy vanishes to second order at its minimum (i.e., D(Q∥π)≈(1/2)χ^2(Q,π) near π), they show that the only possible homomorphism is the logarithm, forcing G=F and Δ=D(Q∥π). The argument is rigorous and relies on standard properties of divergences and convex analysis.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is a characterization theorem: Under the stated hypotheses, the unique decomposition is logZ=−F(Q;p,ℓ)+D(Q∥π). This is an exact identity, not just a bound. The proof does not rely on any specific form of the divergence but uses its second-order behavior near the minimum. The paper also provides counterexamples: if G is not additively separable, one can construct alternative decompositions; if Δ is not required to vanish only at Q=π, other divergences (e.g., α-divergences) can appear; if Δ is not a function of Q and π alone, trivial decompositions exist. These counterexamples clarify the necessity of each hypothesis. The result is significant because it shows that the Gibbs-Bogoliubov decomposition is essentially unique among all decompositions satisfying natural conditions.
strengths: Provides a clean, rigorous characterization of the exact decomposition of logZ, filling a gap in the literature.
The proof is elegant, reducing the problem to a homomorphism and using second-order properties of relative entropy.
Includes explicit counterexamples that demonstrate the necessity of each hypothesis, strengthening the result.
The result is broadly applicable to mean-field theory, Bayesian inference, and statistical physics.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to finite systems; extension to infinite-dimensional or continuous state spaces is not discussed.
The hypotheses, while natural, may not be the only possible ones; other characterizations might exist under different conditions.
The paper does not explore practical implications or algorithmic consequences of the uniqueness result.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly relates to quantum physics and information theory by providing a foundational characterization of variational free energy decompositions. In quantum statistical mechanics, similar variational principles (e.g., Gibbs-Bogoliubov inequality) are used to approximate free energies. The result clarifies the uniqueness of the decomposition, which could inform the development of quantum variational methods. Additionally, the connection to relative entropy and its second-order properties is relevant to quantum information theory, where relative entropy plays a key role in distinguishability and entropy inequalities.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a well-written, technically sound paper that makes a precise contribution to the theory of variational inference and statistical physics. The characterization theorem is novel and complements existing axiomatic approaches. The proof is clear and the counterexamples are instructive. While the scope is limited to finite systems, the result is foundational and likely to be cited in future work on variational methods. The paper is of high quality and significance within its niche.

tldr: This paper demonstrates an adaptive boson sampling architecture that goes beyond linear optics by using measurement-based feedback to realize nonlinear optical evolutions.
motivation: Standard boson sampling relies on linear optical evolution, which is classically simulable in certain regimes; achieving nonlinearity is crucial for demonstrating quantum advantage and enabling new quantum information protocols.
method: The authors implement an adaptive boson sampling setup where measurement outcomes are used to dynamically adjust subsequent optical elements, effectively realizing nonlinear transformations through feedback.
result: They provide witnesses that certify the nonlinear-optical evolution, showing that the output distribution cannot be reproduced by any linear optical circuit.
conclusion: Adaptive boson sampling offers a path to nonlinear quantum optics with potential applications in quantum computing and simulation, though the current demonstration is proof-of-principle.

motivation: Oscillations are a hallmark of nonequilibrium biological processes, and understanding how phase separation influences them is important for cellular regulation.
method: The authors couple ordinary differential equations with a particle-based model to analyze a degradation-mediated negative feedback loop where the final species degrades the first, incorporating phase separation effects.
result: Phase separation can induce oscillations in the feedback loop, altering the dynamics compared to the well-mixed case.

method: They reduce the problem to checking local unitary equivalence of the reduced density matrices of the nondegenerate eigenstates, using invariants derived from the reduced states.
result: They provide necessary and sufficient conditions for local unitary equivalence of the considered class of states, and illustrate with examples.
conclusion: The method simplifies the identification of local unitary equivalence for states with high degeneracy, contributing to entanglement theory.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits using tensor network contraction and Markov processes.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is essential for testing quantum algorithms but faces exponential memory and computational overhead, limiting scalability.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit.
result: The method generates exact samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models.
conclusion: This work significantly expands the scope of classical simulation for quantum algorithm research, enabling validation of assumptions at previously inaccessible scales.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

A video of the physical-level gate sequences for the factorization circuit with distance-3 surfaces. (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17970554)

.
tldr: This paper derives system-level requirements for a controller-decoder system to execute Shor's algorithm with surface code error correction, using realistic superconducting qubit parameters.
motivation: Executing non-Clifford circuits with quantum error correction is a key milestone; understanding the hardware and decoding requirements is essential for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: The authors convert a logical Shor's algorithm circuit for factoring 21 into a surface code circuit, then to physical-level operations, and simulate the full fault-tolerant circuit with realistic parameters.
result: They find that controller-decoder latency must be under tens of microseconds, achievable with distributed decoders, and that near-term hardware with 0.1% error rates and 1000 qubits suffices for successful execution.
conclusion: The outlined requirements guide near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

title: Searching For Quantum Effects In The Brain: A Bell-type Test For Nonclassical Latent Representations In Autoencoders
authors: Iannis K Kominis, Can Xie, Shuguang Li, Michael Skotiniotis And Giorgos P Tsironis
abstract: Whether neural information processing is entirely classical or involves quantum-mechanical elements remains an open question. Here we propose a model-agnostic, information-theoretic test of nonclassicality that bypasses microscopic assumptions and instead probes the structure of neural representations themselves. Using autoencoders as a transparent model system, we introduce a Bell-type consistency test in latent space, and ask whether decoding statistics obtained under multiple readout contexts can be jointly explained by a single positive latent-variable distribution. By shifting the search for quantum-like signatures in neural systems from microscopic dynamics to experimentally testable constraints on information processing, this work opens a new route for probing the fundamental physics of neural computation. The proposed test identifies violations of classical latent-variable consistency at the level of statistical representations, without assuming a specific underlying physical mechanism.
tldr: Proposes a Bell-type consistency test for nonclassical latent representations in autoencoders, searching for quantum-like signatures in neural information processing.
motivation: Whether neural information processing involves quantum effects remains unknown; the paper aims to bypass microscopic assumptions and test nonclassicality at the level of statistical representations.
method: Introduces a Bell-type consistency test in the latent space of autoencoders, checking whether decoding statistics under multiple readout contexts can be explained by a single classical latent-variable distribution.
result: The test identifies violations of classical latent-variable consistency, indicating potential nonclassical signatures in neural representations.
conclusion: This work opens a new route for probing quantum-like effects in neural computation through experimentally testable constraints on information processing.

title: Continuous-Time Random Walk Description Of Anomalous Spin Transport In Dilute Dipolar Networks
authors: Cooper M. Selco, Christian Bengs, Ashok Ajoy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nuclear spin diffusion is often summarized by a single diffusion coefficient, but this coarse-grained description can fail in dilute solids where positional disorder and long-range dipolar couplings generate a broad distribution of hopping rates. We develop a continuous-time random-walk (CTRW) description of [MATH]C polarization transport in natural-abundance diamond (1.1%), constructing the rate matrix from dipolar-mediated flip-flop couplings and sampling exact continuous-time trajectories. Although site-to-site hopping is Markovian, the disorder-averaged dynamics give rise to emergent, anomalous transport. The empirical waiting-time distribution exhibits a heavy tail with exponent [MATH] and exponential cutoff [MATH] s; the mean jump length becomes correlated with the waiting time [MATH] for [MATH] s; and the mean-squared displacement grows sublinearly in both step number and physical time, with exponents [MATH] and [MATH] respectively. We trace the microscopic origin of these signatures to geometric trapping: polarization can rapidly exchange within strongly coupled clusters, including dimers, while weak inter-cluster links control long-range exploration. A kinetic percolation construction links global transport to inter-cluster crossing times, and identifies a corresponding crossing time of [MATH] s, consistent with [MATH]. Finally, mapping paramagnetic impurities onto hard-sphere traps connects the CTRW framework to classic studies of trapping in reaction-diffusion theory and reproduces the qualitative timescale of experimentally measured relaxation, whereas a continuum diffusion equation description does not. These results show that dilute dipolar spin networks require a microscopic, network-resolved transport description beyond the Fickian diffusion equation.
tldr: A continuous-time random walk model captures anomalous spin transport in dilute dipolar networks, revealing subdiffusive behavior and geometric trapping.
motivation: Standard diffusion models fail for dilute solids with disorder and long-range dipolar couplings, motivating a microscopic transport description.
method: Constructed a rate matrix from dipolar flip-flop couplings and simulated exact continuous-time trajectories to compute waiting-time distributions and mean-squared displacement.
result: Disorder-averaged dynamics show heavy-tailed waiting times, correlated jump lengths, and sublinear mean-squared displacement, traced to geometric trapping in clusters.
conclusion: Dilute dipolar spin networks require a network-resolved transport description beyond Fickian diffusion, with implications for spin diffusion in quantum systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates nuclear spin diffusion in dilute dipolar spin networks, specifically focusing on 13C polarization transport in natural-abundance diamond (1.1% 13C). The authors develop a continuous-time random-walk (CTRW) description by constructing the rate matrix from dipolar-mediated flip-flop couplings and sampling exact continuous-time trajectories. They find that although site-to-site hopping is Markovian, disorder-averaged dynamics exhibit emergent anomalous transport. Key signatures include a heavy-tailed waiting-time distribution with exponent α=0.64 and exponential cutoff t_cutoff=19 s, a correlation between mean jump length and waiting time for τ≳0.1 s, and sublinear mean-squared displacement growth in both step number (γ=0.56) and physical time (δ=0.87). The microscopic origin is traced to geometric trapping: rapid exchange within strongly coupled clusters (e.g., dimers) and weak inter-cluster links controlling long-range exploration. A kinetic percolation construction links global transport to inter-cluster crossing times, identifying a crossing time of ~20 s consistent with t_cutoff. Finally, mapping paramagnetic impurities onto hard-sphere traps reproduces the qualitative timescale of experimental relaxation, whereas a continuum diffusion equation fails. The results demonstrate that dilute dipolar spin networks require a microscopic, network-resolved transport description beyond Fickian diffusion.
key_contributions: Develops a CTRW framework for 13C polarization transport in dilute dipolar spin networks, capturing disorder-averaged anomalous transport.
Identifies specific anomalous transport signatures: heavy-tailed waiting-time distribution (α=0.64), correlated jump lengths and waiting times, and sublinear MSD exponents (γ=0.56, δ=0.87).
Provides microscopic explanation via geometric trapping in strongly coupled clusters and weak inter-cluster links, supported by kinetic percolation analysis.
Links CTRW framework to classic trapping in reaction-diffusion theory by mapping paramagnetic impurities onto hard-sphere traps, reproducing experimental relaxation timescales.
Demonstrates the failure of continuum diffusion equation for dilute spin networks, advocating for network-resolved transport descriptions.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a continuous-time random-walk (CTRW) approach, constructing the rate matrix from dipolar-mediated flip-flop couplings in a natural-abundance diamond lattice (1.1% 13C). They sample exact continuous-time trajectories using a kinetic Monte Carlo algorithm, which allows them to compute waiting-time distributions, jump length correlations, and mean-squared displacement (MSD) as functions of step number and physical time. The disorder averaging is performed over many random configurations of 13C spins. To interpret the results, they use a kinetic percolation construction that identifies clusters of strongly coupled spins and computes inter-cluster crossing times. Additionally, they map paramagnetic impurities onto hard-sphere traps to connect with reaction-diffusion theory. The methodology is rigorous and well-suited for studying transport in disordered systems with long-range interactions.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results include the empirical waiting-time distribution exhibiting a heavy tail with exponent α=0.64 and exponential cutoff at t_cutoff=19 s. The mean jump length becomes correlated with waiting time for τ≳0.1 s, indicating that longer waits lead to longer jumps. The MSD grows sublinearly: as a function of step number, MSD ∝ n^γ with γ=0.56, and as a function of time, MSD ∝ t^δ with δ=0.87. These exponents deviate from normal diffusion (γ=1, δ=1), confirming anomalous transport. title: Generating Logical Magic States With The Aid Of non-Abelian Topological Order
authors: Sheng-Jie Huang
Yanzhu Chen
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 16 July 2026;
tldr: This paper proposes a method to generate logical magic states using non-Abelian topological order, specifically Fibonacci anyons, to enable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation.
motivation: Magic states are essential for universal quantum computation, but their generation is challenging. Topological systems offer inherent fault tolerance, and non-Abelian anyons can provide a natural resource for magic states.
method: The authors design a protocol using Fibonacci anyons in a topological system to create logical magic states through braiding and measurement, leveraging the non-Abelian statistics.
result: They demonstrate that logical magic states can be generated with high fidelity using topological operations, potentially reducing the overhead for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
conclusion: Non-Abelian topological order provides a promising platform for generating magic states, advancing the feasibility of universal topological quantum computation.

title: Scaling Of Relaxation And Entropy In Buckled Colloidal Monolayers
authors: Yongming Zhang, Qingyu Qu, Qian-Yuan Tang, And Xiaoguang Ma
abstract:

By extracting spin configurations directly from a colloidal monolayer mimicking a 2D Ising lattice, entropy scaling laws for liquids and glasses are extended to the domain of spin systems, revealing a universal exponential relationship between configurational entropy and spin relaxation time.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 048201] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: Extends entropy scaling laws from liquids and glasses to spin systems using a colloidal monolayer Ising lattice, revealing exponential relation between configurational entropy and spin relaxation time.
motivation: To understand the universal relationship between configurational entropy and relaxation dynamics in disordered systems, extending known scaling laws to spin systems.
method: Experimental extraction of spin configurations from a buckled colloidal monolayer that mimics a 2D Ising lattice, measuring configurational entropy and spin relaxation time.
result: Found a universal exponential relationship between configurational entropy and spin relaxation time, analogous to the Adam-Gibbs relation in glass-forming liquids.
conclusion: The entropy scaling law is universal across different disordered systems, including spin systems, bridging the gap between spin physics and glass physics.

title: From Local Weight Selection To Zeno Slowdown In An Open Su-Schrieffer-Heeger Chain With A Single Local Loss
authors: Y. T. Wang And X. Z. Zhang
abstract:

We study a quadratic open SSH chain with a single-site loss and show that the many-body fermionic Lindblad problem admits an exact reduction to a finite non-Hermitian one-body matrix with a rank-one imaginary impurity. Its rapidities generate the complete Liouvillian spectrum and reveal three mechan…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012457] Published Fri Jul 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the Liouvillian spectrum of an open SSH chain with a single loss, revealing three mechanisms for Zeno slowdown.
motivation: Understanding how local dissipation affects topological systems is important for quantum thermodynamics and open quantum systems.
method: The many-body Lindblad problem is reduced to a non-Hermitian one-body matrix with a rank-one impurity, whose rapidities yield the full Liouvillian spectrum.
result: Three mechanisms for Zeno slowdown are identified: topological edge state protection, band-edge van Hove singularity, and dark state formation.
conclusion: Local loss can induce Zeno slowdown via distinct mechanisms, with implications for controlling dissipation in quantum systems.

authors: Maike Ostmann, Joshua Nunn, And Alex E. Jones

tldr: Proposes a photonic architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing using strong nonlinearities to reduce resource overhead.
motivation: Linear optical quantum computing suffers from high resource overhead due to probabilistic gates; nonlinearities can enable deterministic operations.
method: Integrates strong single-photon nonlinearities into a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger-measurement-based architecture, leveraging cluster states and fault-tolerant protocols.
result: Substantial reduction in resource overhead compared to linear-optics-based architectures, with improved error thresholds.
conclusion: Nonlinear photonic architectures offer a promising path toward scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Expander Quantum Low Density Parity Check Codes Against Long-range Correlated Errors In Memory
authors: Yash Deepak Kashtikar, Pranay Mathur, Sudharsan Senthil, And Avhishek Chatterjee
abstract:

tldr: This paper studies the performance of expander quantum LDPC codes under long-range correlated errors in quantum memory, showing that such codes can achieve fault tolerance with constant space overhead against certain correlated noise models.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum memory typically assumes independent or local errors, but realistic noise can be long-range correlated. Understanding whether constant-overhead codes can handle such errors is crucial for practical quantum computing.
method: The authors analyze the error correction capability of expander quantum LDPC codes under a correlated error model using statistical mechanics mapping and numerical simulations, evaluating logical error rates and thresholds.
result: They find that expander quantum LDPC codes can tolerate long-range correlated errors with constant space overhead, provided the correlations decay sufficiently fast, and they derive conditions for fault tolerance.
conclusion: Expander quantum LDPC codes are promising for fault-tolerant quantum memory even under non-local noise, but the results are specific to certain correlation regimes and may not extend to all practical scenarios.

method: The authors propose a position-resolved quantization scheme that accounts for spatial dependence and losses, likely using a Green's function or mode expansion approach.
result: The framework provides a systematic way to quantize the electromagnetic field in lossy cavities with position-dependent coupling, enabling accurate modeling of quantum optical phenomena.
conclusion: This work advances the theoretical toolkit for cavity quantum electrodynamics in lossy systems, relevant for hybrid quantum systems involving cavity-coupled emitters.

motivation: Understanding quantum chaos and spectral correlations in many-body systems is fundamental, and the spectral form factor is a key diagnostic.
method: The authors analytically compute the spectral form factor using random matrix theory and field-theoretic techniques, extending to leading and beyond-leading order.
result: They obtain explicit expressions for the spectral form factor up to second order in time for all three Dyson symmetry classes (orthogonal, unitary, symplectic).
conclusion: The results provide a detailed characterization of spectral correlations in chaotic quantum many-body systems, confirming universality classes.

tldr: Proposes a method for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D using non-Abelian anyons without braiding.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D typically requires braiding of non-Abelian anyons, which is experimentally challenging. This work aims to achieve universal logic gates without braiding.
method: The authors design a protocol that temporarily moves data into an exotic non-Abelian phase to perform logical gates, leveraging topological properties without physical braiding.
result: They demonstrate that universal fault-tolerant quantum computation is possible in 2D using this approach, avoiding the need for complex braiding operations.
conclusion: This work provides a new pathway toward large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation by simplifying the implementation of logical gates in 2D architectures.

motivation: To enable fault-tolerant quantum computation on exotic topological orders that are not supported by conventional error-correcting codes.
method: Constructs three-dimensional stabilizer codes with single-shot error correction properties, leveraging the geometry and topology of the codes.
result: Demonstrates that the proposed codes can correct errors in a single round of syndrome extraction for fermionic and chiral topological phases.
conclusion: The chiral color code provides a new platform for fault-tolerant quantum computation on exotic topological orders.

method: The authors use parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation with good quantum LDPC codes to reduce overhead.
result: They demonstrate that constant qubit overhead and low time overhead are achievable with their scheme.
conclusion: Good quantum LDPC codes can significantly accelerate fault-tolerant quantum computation, making it more practical.

method: The authors propose a fold-transversal surface code that enables efficient cultivation of magic states through transversal gates and lattice surgery, optimized for architectures with long-range interactions.
result: The protocol achieves significantly lower spacetime overhead compared to standard distillation methods, making it suitable for near-term quantum processors with nonlocal connectivity.
conclusion: Fold-transversal surface code cultivation offers a practical path to reduce resource requirements for fault-tolerant quantum computation, particularly in architectures with nonlocal connectivity.

method: The authors use a cold Rydberg gas with controlled dissipation to map out non-Hermitian spectral topology, measuring winding numbers and scan-direction-dependent nonreciprocity.

conclusion: The work establishes cold Rydberg gases as a platform for studying non-Hermitian topology, but the focus is on topological phases rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

method: The authors propose a beam search decoder that explores multiple candidate error patterns in parallel, pruning unlikely ones to balance accuracy and computational cost.
result: The decoder achieves high decoding accuracy while meeting latency requirements for real-time quantum error correction, avoiding massive classical computation.
conclusion: Beam search decoding is a practical solution for quantum LDPC codes, enabling efficient error correction in near-term quantum computers.

title: Machine Learning Decoding Of Circuit-Level Noise For Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: John Blue, Harshil Avlani, Zhiyang He, Liu Ziyin, And Isaac L. Chuang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2149 (2026).

Fault-tolerant quantum computers will depend crucially on the performance of the classical decoding algorithm which takes in the results of measurements and outputs corrections to the errors inferred to have occurred. Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: This paper applies machine learning decoding to bivariate bicycle codes, a type of quantum LDPC code, achieving lower logical error rates than BP-OSD on small codes but with limited scalability.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient decoders for quantum error correction codes; machine learning decoders have shown promise for surface codes but not yet for QLDPC codes, which are more challenging.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is designed to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes, trained on simulated error data.
result: On the [[144,12,12]] BB code, the ML decoder achieves logical error rates almost 10 times lower than BP-OSD and is an order of magnitude faster, but on larger codes performance degrades.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures or training procedures.

tldr: Develops a unified field-theoretical description of the Bose-Hubbard model capturing low-energy dynamics across the Mott-insulator to superfluid transition, highlighting the failure of cumulant expansions in the superfluid phase.
motivation: To provide a correct low-energy effective theory for the Bose-Hubbard model across the phase transition, addressing quantitative and fundamental failures of existing cumulant expansions.
method: Uses a field-theoretical approach incorporating Berry phase to derive a canonical structure for quantum fluctuations, likely via path integral or effective action methods.
result: Shows that cumulant expansions fail in the superfluid phase both quantitatively and fundamentally, and provides a unified description that captures the correct low-energy dynamics.
conclusion: The Berry-phase-induced canonical structure is essential for correctly describing quantum fluctuations across the Mott-superfluid transition, offering a more accurate theoretical framework.

Quantum phase estimation is a cornerstone algorithm for fault-tolerant quantum computation, especially for electronic structure calculations of chemical systems. Optimal simulation relies on a complex trade-offs across many parameters including Hamiltonian simulation techniques, basis sets, and the …

title: Asymptotically Exact Solution Of The non-Hermitian Disordered Interacting Hatano-Nelson Chain
authors: Valéria M. Mattiello, Victor L. Quito, And Eduardo Miranda
abstract:

This article presents an exact low-energy solution of a one-dimensional model of interacting disordered spinless fermions with non-Hermitian hopping, equivalently formulated as a non-Hermitian spin-1/2 chain. The solution exhibits finite-temperature divergent spin susceptibilities and shows that non-Hermiticity suppresses the entanglement entropy relative to the corresponding Hermitian model, eliminating the associated entanglement scaling.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L032012] Published Wed Jul 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper solves a non-Hermitian disordered interacting fermion chain exactly, showing non-Hermiticity suppresses entanglement entropy.
motivation: To understand the interplay of disorder, interactions, and non-Hermiticity in low-dimensional quantum systems.
method: Exact low-energy solution of the non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson chain with interactions using a mapping to a spin chain.
result: Non-Hermiticity suppresses entanglement entropy and eliminates its scaling, while spin susceptibilities diverge at finite temperature.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2164 (2026).

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars are rare in higher dimensions; the authors aim to provide exact examples in 2D gauge theories.
method: They identify exact eigenstates with a tower structure in a 2D spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs, then use duality to map them to the quantum gauge model.
result: Exact QMBS are found in the 2D quantum gauge model, demonstrating a versatile construction for higher-dimensional scars.
conclusion: The work provides new exact QMBS in 2D, with potential for generalization to other models.

title: High-gain Effects In Broadband Continuous-wave Parametric Down Conversion Sources And Measurements With Undetected Photons
authors: Martin Houde, Franz Roeder, Christine Silberhorn, Benjamin Brecht And Nicolás Quesada
abstract: We study theoretically how high-gain effects affect the measurement outcome of visible signal spectra in undetected photon measurement schemes. We consider two interferometric configurations: firstly, the SU(1,1) interferometer where the idler incurs loss and additional dispersion in between two identical, lossless, squeezers; secondly, the induced coherence interferometer where the idler incurs loss and additional dispersion in between two identical, lossless, squeezers and where the second squeezer is seeded by the idler and a vacuum ancilla mode. Furthermore, we consider a distributed loss configuration where the idler incurs loss as it propagates in the nonlinear medium. Motivated by experimental evidence and due to the fact that broadband sources are ideal for these measurement schemes, we use the dispersive data of a third-order dispersion engineered integrated waveguide parametric down conversion (PDC) source presented in Roeder et al (2024 New J. Phys. 26 123025) to model the PDC spectra in the three configurations. For each configuration we consider the case of idler-only (i) absorption, (ii) additional dispersion, and (iii) the combined effects. We obtain results which outline the strength and weaknesses of the different configurations at different operation points.
tldr: Theoretical study of high-gain effects in broadband continuous-wave parametric down conversion sources for undetected photon measurements.
motivation: To understand how high-gain effects impact measurement outcomes in undetected photon schemes, which are relevant for quantum imaging and sensing.
method: Analyzes two interferometric configurations (SU(1,1) and induced coherence) with loss and dispersion, using a realistic PDC source model.
result: Identifies strengths and weaknesses of each configuration under different operation points, including effects of absorption and dispersion.
conclusion: High-gain effects significantly influence the spectra and must be accounted for in practical implementations of undetected photon measurements.

title: Pseudogauge-Invariant Nonequilibrium Density Operator

Author(s): Francesco Becattini and Carlos Hoyos

We obtain a form of the local thermodynamic equilibrium density operator, which is invariant under pseudogauge transformations of the stress-energy and the spin tensors. This operator is an excellent candidate to describe the dynamics of a system that is assumed to achieve local equilibrium from a p…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 041602] Published Thu Jul 23, 2026.
tldr: The paper constructs a local thermodynamic equilibrium density operator invariant under pseudogauge transformations of stress-energy and spin tensors.
motivation: To describe the dynamics of systems achieving local equilibrium from a relativistic quantum field theory perspective, ensuring gauge invariance of the density operator.
method: The authors derive a form of the local equilibrium density operator that is invariant under pseudogauge transformations by incorporating appropriate constraints.
result: They obtain an operator that remains unchanged under pseudogauge transformations, providing a consistent framework for relativistic thermodynamics.
conclusion: The proposed operator is suitable for modeling local equilibrium in relativistic systems, but the work is highly theoretical and specialized, with limited direct connection to the user's core interests in quantum thermodynamics or information processing.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on dynamics and metastable phases.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium phenomena in strongly correlated electron systems, which may lead to new material properties.
method: Comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances, discussing nonlinear and nonperturbative driving pathways.
result: Identifies key mechanisms for photodoped carrier evolution and emergence of metastable orders like superconducting and magnetic phases.
conclusion: Photoexcitation offers a powerful tool to manipulate Mott insulators, but the work is primarily a review of condensed matter physics without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Efficient Three-dimensional sub-Doppler Cooling Of $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$ In A Penning Trap
authors: Brian J. Mcmahon And Brian C. Sawyer
abstract:
Author(s): Brian J. McMahon and Brian C. Sawyer

The authors demonstrate three-dimensional sub-Doppler cooling of a single
[Phys. Rev. A 114, 013119] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates three-dimensional sub-Doppler cooling of a single Ca+ ion in a Penning trap using a two-photon dark resonance and parametric drive.
motivation: Sub-Doppler cooling in Penning traps is challenging due to the magnetic field and trap geometry; the authors aim to achieve efficient cooling across all motional modes.
method: They exploit a two-photon dark resonance for cooling and apply a parametric drive to the trap electrodes to exchange motional occupations between axial and radial modes, enabling cooling with only axially propagating lasers.
result: Three-dimensional sub-Doppler cooling is achieved, with temperatures below the Doppler limit in all degrees of freedom.

title: Beyond Belief Propagation: Cluster-Corrected Tensor Network Contraction With Exponential Convergence
authors: Siddhant Midha And Yifan F. Zhang

Systematic corrections to belief propagation enable polynomial-time tensor network contraction algorithms while providing rigorous bounds on approximation errors.

tldr: This paper presents a tensor network contraction algorithm with exponential convergence using cluster corrections to belief propagation.
motivation: Tensor network contraction is computationally hard in general; belief propagation provides an approximation but lacks rigorous error bounds. The authors aim to develop a polynomial-time algorithm with provable convergence.
method: They introduce cluster corrections to belief propagation, systematically improving the approximation by considering local correlations, and prove exponential convergence of the error.
