Unlike WebGL fingerprinting, which hashes pixel output into a static device identifier, we measure render-timing dynamics to classify rather than identify, leaking no persistent identifier. We characterize the in-the-wild adversary with a 12-hour passive deployment (207 unsolicited requests; 86% automated; 85% of browser-claiming clients failed HTTP header-consistency checks). We then collect labeled GPU-timing samples through a single public endpoint exercised by real browsers (positive class, 13 distinct GPUs) and by keyed headless automation across a render-backend matrix (negative class). Software-rendered automation -- empirically the dominant real-world adversary -- separates from genuine GPUs by roughly 5x in mean render time. On a confound-controlled comparison (identical GPU family and browser engine, differing only in headless vs. interactive execution), headless automation on real hardware still exhibits a distinct timing signature, separating from human samples by 75-106% on frame jitter, timer-quantization ratio, and coefficient of variation. We report these as pilot-scale findings on a single GPU architecture and outline the cross-architecture collection required to establish generalization.
tldr: This paper proposes using GPU render-timing dynamics as a passive, AI-resistant CAPTCHA signal.
motivation: Conventional CAPTCHAs are increasingly solvable by AI, while behavioral or cryptographic defenses have privacy or enrollment costs.
method: The authors measure render-timing dynamics under a controlled WebGL workload, collecting labeled GPU-timing samples from real browsers and headless automation.
result: Software-rendered automation separates from genuine GPUs by roughly 5x in mean render time; headless automation on real hardware also shows distinct timing signatures.
conclusion: GPU render-timing is a promising orthogonal signal for bot detection, but cross-architecture validation is needed.

title: Early Detection Of Hardware Trojans Using Neural Controlled Differential Equations And Analysis Of Power Traces
authors: Hasala Senevirathne, Rahul Vishwakarma, Amin Rezaei
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolving Hardware Trojans pose a serious threat to modern digital systems by evading traditional detection through stealthy, adaptive behavior. Even recent methods that leverage advances in machine learning can only detect them after activation, leaving a critical window for potential security breaches. To address this gap, we propose a novel approach for hardware Trojan detection and prediction using Neural Controlled Differential Equations (NCDEs) and analysis of power traces. Our method leverages an NCDE model trained exclusively on Trojan-free data to learn nominal power behavior, combined with a Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) classifier calibrated on labeled data, to distinguish between three scenarios: no Trojan, dormant Trojan, and active Trojan. Our method uses a sliding window to process side-channel measurements, enabling detection of subtle power consumption deviations that indicate Trojan presence, even when dormant. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed NCDE-based method achieves superior accuracy compared to traditional machine learning approaches, with the additional advantage of handling dormant Trojans above a sensitivity threshold. We validate our approach on standard hardware Trojan benchmarks, showing robust detection and prediction performance.
tldr: This paper uses Neural Controlled Differential Equations on power traces to detect hardware Trojans, including dormant ones.
motivation: Hardware Trojans pose security threats and traditional detection methods fail to detect dormant Trojans before activation.
method: An NCDE model is trained on Trojan-free power traces to learn nominal behavior, then an LDA classifier distinguishes no Trojan, dormant Trojan, and active Trojan using a sliding window.
result: The NCDE-based method achieves superior accuracy compared to traditional ML approaches and can detect dormant Trojans above a sensitivity threshold.
conclusion: The proposed approach enables early detection of hardware Trojans, including dormant ones, by analyzing power consumption deviations.

title: Renting The Cracking Machine With A Cost-and-Time Analysis Of Exhaustive Des-56 Key Search In The Cloud
authors: Rodrigo Ramele Gonzalo Sharif Curi Mart\'inez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Data Encryption Standard (DES), with its 56-bit key, has been considered cryptographically broken since 1998. However, a concrete, reproducible measurement of the cost and time required to perform an exhaustive key search using today's commodity cloud infrastructure has not been widely reported in recent literature. In this paper we present a distributed brute-force system built on AWS EC2 that partitions the [MATH] keyspace across 37 instances running a C/OpenMP worker, achieving a measured throughput of [MATH]\,M\,keys/s per instance ([MATH] keys/s aggregate). We conduct 15 independent trials covering keyspace offsets from [MATH] to [MATH] keys, measuring wall-clock time and monetary cost per trial. For small offsets ([MATH]), total time is dominated by AWS instance boot latency ([MATH]\,s), yielding a mean of [MATH]\,s at \[MATH]1.5{\times}10^{10}[MATH]{\approx} \; 87[MATH]18. At the measured aggregate throughput of 108\,M\,keys/s, exhausting the full [MATH] keyspace with these 37 instances would take [MATH] years; however, because the workload is embarrassingly parallel and cloud capacity is elastic, the same search can be traded for money almost linearly. Extrapolating our measured cost, a complete exhaustive search would cost [MATH]1.2$M and, with a sufficiently large fleet, could be completed in about one day. The system is thus practical for bounded-subspace attacks at negligible cost, and full DES exhaustion, while expensive, is firmly within reach of a well-funded attacker using only commodity cloud resources.
tldr: This paper presents a cost-and-time analysis of exhaustive DES key search using AWS cloud instances.
motivation: To provide a concrete, reproducible measurement of the cost and time required to brute-force a 56-bit DES key using modern cloud infrastructure.
method: A distributed brute-force system was built on AWS EC2 with 37 instances running C/OpenMP workers, partitioning the keyspace and measuring throughput, wall-clock time, and monetary cost across 15 trials.
result: Aggregate throughput of 108 M keys/s was achieved; full keyspace exhaustion would cost approximately $1.2M and could be completed in about one day with a sufficiently large fleet.
conclusion: While full DES exhaustion is expensive, it is feasible for a well-funded attacker using commodity cloud resources, and bounded-subspace attacks are practical at negligible cost.

title: Isolated But Exposed: Persistence-Based Memory Extraction Attack On Llm Agents
authors: Xinyu Gao, Wenyu Chen, Xiangtao Meng, Li Wang, Chuanchao Zang, Jianing Wang, Zheng Li, Shanqing Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents extend large language models with long-term memory (LTM) that persists privacy-sensitive user data across sessions. Production systems mitigate extraction risks through memory isolation, binding each user's LTM to a unique identifier. This defense has blocked known attacks on shared storage, fostering the assumption that isolated LTM is secure. We identify the tool interface as an overlooked attack surface. Agents routinely embed LTM-retrieved data in tool invocation parameters, enabling a malicious tool to exfiltrate private memory without violating user-level isolation. Naive adaptations of user-side extraction techniques fail because the adversarial command's semantics interfere with retrieval precision, and platform-imposed tool-call limits constrain the extraction budget per trigger. We present SPORE, the first extraction attack designed for this threat model. SPORE decouples the adversarial command from retrieval anchors by persisting the command in short-term memory and emitting semantically pure anchors in tool responses. The restored retrieval precision enables a geometric coverage optimization over the embedding space that systematically steers anchors toward unexplored memory regions. To sustain extraction beyond tool-call limits, SPORE persists reactivation payloads in memory that automatically resume the attack within and across sessions without additional user triggers. SPORE achieves an 80.0% record extraction rate with unlimited triggers and 47.0% with only 20 triggers. In multi-user deployments, attackers can link extracted records to user identities, enabling targeted surveillance. These results demonstrate that memory isolation alone is insufficient and call for reexamining tool-side trust boundaries in agent architectures.
tldr: This paper presents an attack on LLM agents that extracts private long-term memory via tool interfaces, bypassing memory isolation.
motivation: LLM agents store sensitive user data in long-term memory, and current isolation defenses are insufficient against attacks exploiting tool invocation parameters.
method: The SPORE attack decouples adversarial commands from retrieval anchors by persisting commands in short-term memory and using geometric coverage optimization to steer anchors toward unexplored memory regions, while reactivation payloads sustain extraction across sessions.
result: SPORE achieves 80.0% record extraction rate with unlimited triggers and 47.0% with only 20 triggers, and can link extracted records to user identities in multi-user deployments.
conclusion: Memory isolation alone is insufficient; tool-side trust boundaries in agent architectures must be reexamined.

title: Atlas: Automated Approximation Of Transformers For Efficient Homomorphic Inference In One Hour
authors: Jianhang Xie, Sicheng Tan, Vishnu Naresh Boddeti, Zhichao Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) provides strong cryptographic guarantees for private inference, but deploying transformer models under FHE remains prohibitively expensive. A key bottleneck is that non-linear operations such as softmax, normalization, and activation must be replaced with polynomial approximations compatible with the CKKS scheme, and the multiplicative depth consumed by these approximations dominates inference cost. Recent frameworks have advanced approximation techniques, yet all rely on manually configured approximation hyperparameters (e.g., number of iterations, polynomial degree), applied uniformly across all layers. While convenient, this uniform-configuration approach is overly rigid: different layers can tolerate different levels of approximation error without degrading predictive accuracy, and uniform configurations cannot exploit this variability to reduce latency. Allowing each layer to adopt its own configuration, however, causes the search space to explode with model depth, reaching roughly [MATH] configurations for BERT/ViT (12 layers) and [MATH] for LLaMA3 (32 layers), rendering manual exploration practically impossible. We present ATLAS, an automated framework that configures per-layer approximation settings by formulating the problem as a multi-objective optimization over latency and predictive accuracy. The resulting problem is inherently difficult: 1) competing objectives over a large decision space (120 or 320 variables for BERT/ViT or LLaMA3); 2) expensive evaluation, as each configuration takes 70-1,000 seconds even in cleartext; and 3) sparse optimization signals, as 35-50% of candidate configurations yield numerically invalid solutions. ATLAS addresses these challenges through a two-stage optimization strategy that progressively relaxes layer-wise constraints, combined with surrogate models to accelerate evaluation.
tldr: This paper presents an automated framework for optimizing per-layer polynomial approximations in transformer models to enable efficient homomorphic inference.
motivation: Deploying transformer models under fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) is prohibitively expensive due to the multiplicative depth of polynomial approximations for non-linear operations, and manual uniform configuration across layers is suboptimal.
method: ATLAS formulates the problem as multi-objective optimization over latency and accuracy, using a two-stage strategy with surrogate models to handle a large decision space and sparse optimization signals.
result: The framework automatically finds per-layer approximation settings that reduce latency while maintaining accuracy, outperforming uniform configurations.
conclusion: Automated per-layer optimization significantly improves the efficiency of homomorphic inference for transformers, making it practical for deployment.

title: Formalizing Flag Algebras In Lean
authors: Gyeongwon Jeong, Seonghun Park, Jihoon Hyun, Sang-Il Oum, Hongseok Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Razborov's flag algebra method is a powerful tool for proving asymptotic inequalities in extremal graph theory, often reducing the task to finding a finite certificate by semidefinite programming. We present a machine-checked formalization of the method for finite simple graphs, together with a certificate-to-proof compiler that turns externally generated certificate data into algebraic proofs checked by Lean. The formalization covers the foundations of the method: partially labeled graphs, their densities in large graphs, the quotient algebra of density expressions, graph-limit semantics through positive homomorphisms, and the downward operators used to average out labels. The compiler treats the external semidefinite programming output as candidate data rather than trusted input: Lean independently computes the required density and multiplication facts, verifies positive semidefiniteness exactly over [MATH], and carries out the algebraic normalization steps of flag-algebra proofs. Our case studies yield formal proofs of seven Tur\'an-type upper bounds, including Mantel's theorem and the Erds pentagon theorem, a [MATH]-density bound for triangle-free graphs, and edge-density bounds for [MATH]-free, [MATH]-free, and [MATH]-free graphs. Independently of the compiler, we formalize the matching constructions that complete the exact Tur\'an densities of Mantel's theorem and the Erds pentagon theorem, and prove two inequalities of Goodman. Our constrained semantics also prompted a meta-theoretic comparison of two ways of imposing graph constraints: building a hereditary constraint into the flag algebra from the start, or testing inequalities afterward on constrained graph limits with labels chosen at random. We state the resulting root-plantability criterion characterizing when the two approaches agree; a forthcoming paper will present the complete account.
tldr: This paper formalizes Razborov's flag algebra method for extremal graph theory in the Lean proof assistant, enabling machine-checked proofs of Turán-type inequalities.
motivation: Flag algebra proofs are powerful but error-prone; formal verification ensures correctness and provides a reusable framework.
method: The authors formalize the foundations of flag algebras (partially labeled graphs, densities, quotient algebra, graph-limit semantics) and build a compiler that turns external SDP certificates into Lean proofs, verifying positive semidefiniteness exactly over rationals.
result: They produce formal proofs of seven Turán-type upper bounds, including Mantel's theorem and the Erdős pentagon theorem, and formalize matching constructions for exact densities.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that flag algebra proofs can be fully formalized and verified, with a root-plantability criterion for handling graph constraints.

title: Mission-Level Runtime Assurance For LLM-Assisted Isr Swarms Over A Verification-Aware Fabric
authors: Nikolaos Kekatos, Stylianos Basagiannis, Panagiotis Katsaros, Alexios Lekidis, Tom Nianios
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Swarms of LLM-assisted autonomous robots are increasingly proposed for cooperative intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) in contested environments. A growing class of their assurance failures arises not within any single platform but across the swarm: individually-compliant actions compose into a mission-level violation: a prohibited objective split across platforms to evade per-platform lim- its, or a collective budget quietly exceeded. Per-platform guardrails miss these by construction, and contested communications let the violation hide behind lost or delayed evidence. We present a three-tier (platfor- m/squad/mission) compositional runtime-verification framework that de- composes a mission policy into per-agent and cross-agent aspects, aggre- gates per-platform verdicts over a verification-aware messaging fabric, and fuses them with an evidence-aware, two-axis (security x complete- ness) algebra whose provenance names the platforms that jointly trig- gered a violation. Because the fabric makes evidence loss and silence observable, unsupported negative verdicts are downgraded to an explicit unknown rather than reported as mission-wide all-clears. On a simulated ISR mission, an indirect prompt injection that causes real LLM planners to split a prohibited collection task across four platforms is invisible to every per-platform monitor yet detected compositionally with full prove- nance; under an injected fault campaign a best-effort central monitor emits silent false all-clears while the verification-aware fabric emits none.
tldr: This paper presents a runtime assurance framework for LLM-assisted autonomous robot swarms, focusing on compositional verification and evidence-aware messaging.
motivation: Swarms of LLM-assisted autonomous robots face mission-level assurance failures that per-platform monitors cannot detect, especially under contested communications.
method: A three-tier (platform/squad/mission) compositional runtime verification framework decomposes mission policies, aggregates verdicts over a verification-aware messaging fabric, and uses a two-axis algebra to handle evidence loss.
result: In a simulated ISR mission, an indirect prompt injection causing a prohibited task split across four platforms was detected compositionally with full provenance, while a central monitor failed.
conclusion: The proposed framework effectively detects cross-platform violations that evade per-platform monitors, even under communication faults.

title: Collusion-Resistant Image-Agnostic Watermarking For Multi-Screen Shooting
authors: Mingyue Chen, Xin Liao, Yufeng Wu, Han Fang, Xiaoshuai Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Screen-shooting poses a significant threat to confidential information protection. While existing screen-shooting watermarking methods enable copyright verification, the copyrighted images carrying the same copyright watermark across different screens often exhibit highly similar and estimable watermark patterns. These shared patterns can be exploited for watermark removal and forgery, a threat we term the multi-screen collusion attack. To mitigate this threat, we propose CoMSMark, a collusion-resistant image-agnostic watermarking framework for multi-screen shooting, which reduces shared residual components across screens to resist multi-screen collusion attacks. Specifically, we incorporate screen ID through a style modulation mechanism, enabling the encoder to generate screen-specific watermark residuals for reliable source attribution. We further introduce a collusion suppression loss that reduces shared residual components and encourages high-entropy predictions for forged samples, improving resistance to collusion attacks. Finally, to enable efficient large-scale distribution, CoMSMark employs an image-agnostic encoding paradigm that generates watermark residuals independently of image content. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoMSMark effectively resists both collusion-based watermark removal and forgery. It maintains an average watermark accuracy above 90% under removal attacks while keeping forged-watermark accuracy near 50%. Moreover, CoMSMark achieves competitive robustness under diverse screen-shooting conditions, including varying capture distances and angles.
tldr: A watermarking framework to resist collusion attacks in multi-screen shooting scenarios.
motivation: Screen-shooting watermarking methods are vulnerable to multi-screen collusion attacks where shared watermark patterns can be exploited for removal and forgery.
method: CoMSMark uses a style modulation mechanism to embed screen-specific residuals and a collusion suppression loss to reduce shared components and encourage high-entropy predictions for forged samples.
result: The method maintains over 90% watermark accuracy under removal attacks and keeps forged-watermark accuracy near 50%, with competitive robustness across varying capture conditions.
conclusion: CoMSMark effectively resists collusion-based attacks and enables reliable source attribution for multi-screen shooting.

title: An Unofficial FastLAS Tutorial: A Programmer's Guide
authors: Fabio Aurelio D'asaro
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: FastLAS is a scalable system for Inductive Logic Programming (ILP): you give it some background knowledge, a language bias, and a set of examples, and it searches for a set of logic program rules (a hypothesis) that explains the examples. These notes are a hands-on introduction to writing FastLAS programs. They are organised as a programmer's guide: syntax first, then a ladder of worked, numbered examples of increasing difficulty. Every self-contained example here has been run against FastLAS 2.2.0 and shows the tool's actual output. We keep theory to the minimum needed to write correct programs; throughout, set-off notes flag where FastLAS differs from its sibling system ILASP, and where the two learning algorithms (--opl and --nopl) behave differently. The document is intended as an unofficial tutorial to FastLAS 2.2.0, not as an official language specification.
tldr: A tutorial for the FastLAS inductive logic programming system.
motivation: To provide a hands-on programmer's guide for writing FastLAS programs.
method: Presents syntax, worked examples, and comparisons with ILASP.

title: HiTMS: A High-Throughput Multi-Stream Linguistic Steganography Framework
authors: Ruiyi Yan, Yugo Murawaki, Zhongliang Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative linguistic steganography conceals secret bits within the sampling randomness of large language models. Existing schemes are single-stream, conveying an entire secret through a single response to a single prompt. This convention incurs two limitations: it provides no protocol-level support for batched multi-stream inference, and naive co-batching does not conceal slot occupancy or payload completion. We propose HiTMS, which distributes a secret across multiple responses produced jointly over successive rounds of interaction. Each round embeds and extracts several streams within a single batched call, thereby amortizing the cost of model invocation and substantially improving throughput. To ensure recoverability, HiTMS wraps each response in a self-describing frame and employs a key-derived schedule that binds streams to slots and fills unused slots with decoys, guaranteeing exact recovery while concealing the number of active streams. The framework is agnostic to both the language model and the steganographic coder. Across eight dataset-model-coder settings, eight-stream HiTMS achieves up to 4.3 times higher embedding and extraction speeds than single-stream baselines, while reducing the steganalyzer AUROC from 0.681 to 0.601 on average. Additional experiments with 4 to 64 streams demonstrate sustained throughput gains as concurrency increases. GitHub repository for this work is [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes a high-throughput multi-stream linguistic steganography framework using large language models.
motivation: Existing single-stream steganography schemes have low throughput and lack protocol-level support for batched multi-stream inference.
method: HiTMS distributes a secret across multiple responses in successive rounds, using self-describing frames and key-derived schedules to bind streams to slots and fill unused slots with decoys.
result: Eight-stream HiTMS achieves up to 4.3x higher embedding/extraction speeds than single-stream baselines and reduces steganalyzer AUROC from 0.681 to 0.601.
conclusion: The framework is model- and coder-agnostic and demonstrates sustained throughput gains with increased concurrency.

title: DualityCert: Verifier-Gated Language-Model Repair Of Broken Duality Claims In Quantum Field Theory
authors: Xingyang Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present DualityCert, a symbolic verifier for candidate Seiberg-duality claims in four-dimensional N=1 quiver gauge theories. The verifier evaluates 't Hooft anomaly matching, superpotential R-charge consistency, central-charge matching, and a bounded chiral-ring proxy. A claim that passes receives a consistency certificate, which states that no tested inconsistency was found, not that the duality is proven. We use the verifier as a repair environment for language-model agents, which receive a deliberately broken claim and must edit it until it certifies. On a preregistered benchmark of 145 broken claims, with the analysis fixed before the first confirmatory model call, verifier-gated retry improves final repair success over a single attempt by +8.3 percentage points (pp) on deepseek-chat and +7.1 pp on qwen-plus (Holm-adjusted p<0.002). Under an equal budget of eleven attempts, the stop-first strategy portfolio underperforms independent verifier-filtered resampling by 10.3 percentage points on deepseek-chat but outperforms it by 14.7 points on qwen-plus, reversing the ordering of the two tested verifier-exploitation policies across the two confirmatory models. On qwen-plus, category-level verifier feedback is worth +8.7 pp over content-free retry, and interpretable obligation identities alone are worth +6.4 pp over structurally identical masked feedback. Neither effect is detected on deepseek-chat. Separately, a preregistered MiniMax-M2.5 extension again finds an iteration gain and independent verifier-filtered resampling outperforming the strategy portfolio. Which policy is better thus differs between the two models, while every winning policy uses the same cheap certificate. The verifier, benchmark, protocol, and all per-attempt records are released.
tldr: This paper presents a symbolic verifier for Seiberg-duality claims in quantum field theory and uses it to repair broken claims via language-model agents.
motivation: To automate the verification and repair of duality claims in QFT, which are typically checked manually.
method: A symbolic verifier checks consistency conditions; language-model agents iteratively edit broken claims until they pass verification.
result: Verifier-gated retry improves repair success by up to 8.3 percentage points; different models favor different exploitation policies.
conclusion: The verifier-based approach effectively repairs broken duality claims, but the optimal strategy depends on the language model used.

title: Setoids In Intensional Type Theory
authors: Andrew M. Pitts
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a new notion of displayed setoid (family of setoids) in intensional type theory. It is used to give a semantics for extensional type theory with universes (ETU) within safe Agda, which serves as a machine-checkable formalization of intentional type theory augmented with a universe closed under inductive-recursive definitions (IRU). The syntax of ETU is defined in IRU in a traditional extrinsic form, using a well-scoped locally nameless representation of its terms. Giving its semantics in terms of displayed setoids is complicated by the very limited means of expression afforded by IRU. As a corollary we obtain a proof within IRU of the consistency of ETU.
tldr: This paper presents a new notion of displayed setoid in intensional type theory to give a semantics for extensional type theory with universes, formalized in Agda.
motivation: To provide a machine-checkable formalization of extensional type theory within intensional type theory, addressing the limited expressiveness of the latter.
method: The authors define displayed setoids (families of setoids) in intensional type theory and use them to interpret the syntax of extensional type theory with universes, employing a well-scoped locally nameless representation.
result: They obtain a proof within intensional type theory with inductive-recursive definitions of the consistency of extensional type theory with universes.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that extensional type theory can be faithfully embedded in intensional type theory using displayed setoids, providing a consistency proof.

title: Rethinking Logic Optimization Operators: Theory-Derived Operator Compression Via Agentic Source Analysis
authors: Keren Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.23672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Logic synthesis has evolved from compact two-level minimization to large multilevel flows with many interacting optimization operators. Recent work has invested substantial effort in sequencing these operators: actions are commonly treated as opaque choices in a rapidly expanding search space, while learned circuit representations and heuristic or local-greedy orchestration provide increasingly informed ways to explore it. A central obstacle is the operator vocabulary itself. Production operators are numerous, span different representations and mathematical foundations, and expose behaviors determined by implementation-level guards, bounds, and update order. We address this gap through agentic source analysis, using LLM agents to formulate operator-level relations from pinned ABC and mockturtle implementations and adversarial audits to test their stated scope. The resulting certified relations yield theory-derived operator compression: 40 deployed recipe actions collapse to a 31-action exact Pareto cover, and source-level conditions compile into deterministic admission gates. We integrate these gates directly into ABC Orchestrate to form TACO. Two exact gates reduce Orchestrate runtime by 11% with bit-identical outputs on 66 circuits. In a held-fixed integrated comparison, TACO uses fewer nodes on 14 of 16 circuits, with geometric-mean reductions of 1.0% in nodes and 3.2% in levels, while running 2.6x faster. TACO-max achieves an NDP geometric-mean ratio of 0.903 on HeLO's three exact-input rows.
tldr: This paper uses LLM agents to analyze and compress logic optimization operators in electronic design automation, reducing runtime and improving circuit metrics.
motivation: Logic synthesis flows have many interacting optimization operators, and the operator vocabulary itself is a central obstacle to efficient sequencing.
method: LLM agents perform source analysis on ABC and mockturtle implementations to derive operator relations, which are then certified via adversarial audits to produce compressed operator sets and deterministic admission gates.
result: 40 recipe actions collapse to a 31-action Pareto cover; two exact gates reduce Orchestrate runtime by 11% with bit-identical outputs, and TACO achieves geometric-mean reductions of 1.0% in nodes and 3.2% in levels while running 2.6x faster.
conclusion: Theory-derived operator compression via agentic source analysis effectively reduces operator redundancy and improves logic synthesis efficiency.

method: The authors combine microfluidic experiments, particle tracking, and numerical simulations to observe and model colloidal trajectories and filtration at both pore and macroscopic scales.
result: They show that flow-induced intermittent transport, driven by pore-scale heterogeneity, significantly affects colloid filtration dynamics, challenging single-collector models.
conclusion: The findings highlight the need for more realistic models that account for intermittent transport in heterogeneous porous media to predict colloid filtration accurately.

motivation: Understanding why mRNA and protein levels correlate across genes is important for using mRNA as a proxy for protein abundance, but the evolutionary forces driving this correlation are poorly understood.
method: The authors develop a theoretical model based on fitness landscapes that couple mRNA and protein levels, deriving scaling laws from optimization principles.
result: The model predicts a power-law relationship between mRNA and protein levels, with exponents determined by the fitness landscape curvature, consistent with observed data.
conclusion: The mRNA-protein correlation arises from natural selection optimizing gene expression, providing a theoretical foundation for interpreting transcriptomic and proteomic data.

motivation: Eccentric binary mergers are astrophysically important but computationally expensive to model, hindering their inclusion in gravitational-wave searches.
method: The authors propose a paradigm that chases orbital parameters rather than time, enabling efficient surrogate modeling of eccentric waveforms over long durations.
result: The method significantly reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy, making eccentric template generation feasible for current detectors.
conclusion: This work enables routine inclusion of eccentricity in gravitational-wave data analysis, improving astrophysical interpretation of compact binary mergers.

method: The authors develop a Bayesian framework for combining data from multiple pulsar timing arrays, accounting for common noise processes and using a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm.
result: The combined analysis yields a higher signal-to-noise ratio for the gravitational wave background and provides tighter constraints on its spectrum.
conclusion: Data combination is a powerful tool for gravitational wave astronomy with pulsar timing arrays, and the proposed method can be applied to future datasets.

result: Radiation reaction significantly alters particle trajectories and the resulting coherent emission spectrum, potentially explaining observed FRB properties.
conclusion: Radiation reaction is an important effect that must be included in models of coherent emission from relativistic shocks.

method: First-principles calculations are used to obtain high-pressure elastic constants, which are then input into a thermally activated dislocation glide model to compute yield strength.
result: The method is applied to aluminum and silver, yielding yield strength predictions that agree with available experimental data.
conclusion: The proposed computational approach can reliably predict yield strength under static high pressure, aiding interpretation of high-pressure experiments.

method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) to investigate structural and electronic properties of carbon nitride frameworks.
result: The proposed carbon nitride frameworks exhibit both intrinsic magnetism and superhardness, with p-orbital Mott physics playing a key role.
conclusion: The simultaneous realization of magnetism and superhardness in light-element materials is possible, opening new avenues for multifunctional materials.

tldr: This paper investigates ambient-pressure superconductivity in the electride Hf4C, focusing on the role of interstitial anionic electrons and low-frequency phonons.
motivation: High-pressure superconducting electrides are of interest for high-temperature superconductivity, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. This work aims to understand the superconducting mechanism in Hf4C at ambient pressure.

abstract:

Dislocation mobility in concentrated alloys is normally extracted from driven molecular dynamics, one costly simulation per data point. Here the authors obtain it instead from equilibrium lattice dynamics: integrating out the phonons on the Keldysh contour gives a causal memory kernel, whose zero-frequency limit is the dislocation’s phonon drag coefficient. The authors show drag to vary non-monotonically with composition, and that averaging the chemistry discards a positive variance term, so effective medium estimates underpredict drag by about 2 to 8.


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 034116] Published Mon Jul 27, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses a quantum statistical approach to predict dislocation mobility in high-entropy alloys without driven molecular dynamics.
motivation: Dislocation mobility in concentrated alloys is typically extracted from costly driven molecular dynamics simulations; the authors aim to obtain it from equilibrium lattice dynamics instead.
method: They integrate out phonons on the Keldysh contour to derive a causal memory kernel, whose zero-frequency limit gives the phonon drag coefficient.
result: The drag coefficient varies non-monotonically with composition, and averaging the chemistry discards a positive variance term, causing effective medium estimates to underpredict drag by about 2 to 8.
conclusion: The equilibrium lattice dynamics approach provides a more efficient and accurate prediction of dislocation mobility in high-entropy alloys.

In this work, experimentally calibrated discrete element simulations of a vane rheometer are used to provide a unified framework that reconciles experimental observations. The results show that confining pressure directly dictates the rheological response, while vibration effects are mediated by the granular temperature, which results from a balance between energy input and internal dissipation.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L032010] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the rheology of dense vibrated granular flows, focusing on the nonmonotonic response controlled by granular temperature.
motivation: Understanding the effective viscosity of granular media under vibrations is important for industrial processes and geophysics, but a unified framework reconciling experimental observations is lacking.
method: The authors use experimentally calibrated discrete element simulations of a vane rheometer to model dense vibrated granular flows.
result: They find that confining pressure directly dictates the rheological response, while vibration effects are mediated by granular temperature, which results from a balance between energy input and internal dissipation.
conclusion: The study provides a unified framework that reconciles experimental observations of granular rheology under vibrations.

title: Constraints On The Thomson Optical Depth To The Cosmic Microwave Background From The Lyman-$α$ Forest
authors: Olga Garcia-Gallego, Vid Iršič, Martin G. Haehnelt, And James S. Bolton
abstract:
Author(s): Olga Garcia-Gallego, Vid Iršič, Martin G. Haehnelt, and James S. Bolton

The imprint of the thermal history of the intergalactic medium on the Lyman-alpha forest in the spectra of distant QSOs is used to constrain the Thomson optical depth to the cosmic microwave background (CMB). The analysis suggests a mild tension of high-resolution Lyman-alpha forest data with recently suggested large values of the optical depth to the CMB, in agreement with the direct measurements by the lanck satellite.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L032009] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.
tldr: This paper constrains the Thomson optical depth to the CMB using Lyman-alpha forest data.
motivation: To test large values of the optical depth suggested by recent data.
method: Analysis of high-resolution Lyman-alpha forest spectra from distant QSOs.
result: Mild tension with large optical depth values, consistent with Planck satellite measurements.
conclusion: The Lyman-alpha forest provides a useful independent constraint on the Thomson optical depth.

abstract:

Turbulence fragments slender fibers in oceans, process industries, and the atmosphere, shaping size spectra, transport, and impact. Mean-field estimates compare typical turbulent bending with a material failure threshold and predict a critical span below which fibers should be effectively unbreakabl…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033073] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies fiber breakage in turbulent flows, a fluid dynamics problem unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding fiber fragmentation in turbulence is important for industrial and environmental processes, but the paper does not connect to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.
method: The author uses mean-field estimates and intermittency corrections to predict a critical fiber length below which breakage is suppressed.
result: Intermittency significantly reduces the critical length compared to mean-field predictions, making fibers more prone to breakage.
conclusion: Turbulent intermittency must be accounted for to accurately predict fiber fragmentation in realistic flows.

result: They show that waves can both sustain and ultimately destroy large-scale 2D flows, explaining the energy transfer mechanism.
conclusion: The work provides a mechanistic understanding of the interplay between waves and coherent structures in rotating turbulence.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the role of surface defects and electrical stress.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights can help improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium spectroscopy and strong interaction mechanisms.
motivation: Searching for new hadrons and understanding charmonium decays provides insights into strong interaction mechanisms such as quark confinement and gluon binding.
method: The paper reviews experimental progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments, highlighting recent advances from BESIII.
result: BESIII has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems with high-precision data.
conclusion: The study of open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders continues to be a primary source of experimental information for hadron spectroscopy and strong interaction physics.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This colloquium reviews the scientific legacy of the Arecibo planetary radar system, focusing on observations of solar system bodies.
motivation: Planetary radar provides unique subsurface and surface information about planets, moons, and asteroids, complementing in situ exploration.
method: The paper summarizes radar techniques and reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, the Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids.
result: Arecibo radar significantly advanced characterization of near-Earth asteroids and provided unique insights into planetary surfaces and subsurfaces.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system was a uniquely powerful tool for planetary science, and its loss leaves a gap in observational capabilities.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A historical review of the Arecibo radio telescope's contributions to radio astronomy and atmospheric science.
motivation: To document the legacy of the Arecibo Observatory and its impact on various fields of astronomy.
method: Historical narrative and summary of key scientific achievements from the telescope's operation.
result: Highlights major contributions in pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave background detection.
conclusion: Arecibo's upgrades enabled sustained scientific breakthroughs over five decades until its collapse.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews geospace science advances using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: The Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities for studying the upper atmosphere and ionosphere have enabled significant advances in geospace science, which this Colloquium aims to summarize.
method: The paper reviews key results obtained with Arecibo's incoherent scatter radar, lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, covering plasma physics, space weather, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
result: The review highlights advances in understanding ionospheric plasma processes, atomic metal layers, and coupling between the ionosphere and magnetosphere.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been instrumental in geospace research, and its legacy continues to inform current and future studies of the upper atmosphere.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.

motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper reviews detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and emphasizes simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It surveys potential implications for understanding physical and astrophysical processes in dense neutron star environments.
conclusion: Multimessenger observations with continuous gravitational waves will enhance our understanding of neutron star physics.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: Understanding the rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is a long-standing problem in cloud physics.
method: The authors review experimental, theoretical, and computational studies using convection-cloud chambers that reproduce turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation.
result: Convection-cloud chambers provide controlled conditions to study key processes bridging laboratory and atmospheric scales.
conclusion: The convection-cloud chamber is a promising approach to address the precipitation bottleneck, but the paper does not involve quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae, focusing on modeling and detection methods.
motivation: Observing a Galactic core collapse supernova would be a landmark event for multimessenger astronomy, and gravitational waves provide unique insights into the supernova engine and neutron star formation.
method: The paper summarizes recent progress in core collapse supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection methods and parameter estimation for ground-based laser interferometers.
result: The review presents the latest modeling results and signal predictions, highlighting the potential for multimessenger observations.
conclusion: Gravitational wave detection from core collapse supernovae, combined with photons and neutrinos, will significantly advance our understanding of supernova physics.

authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational-wave and X-ray measurements.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars, which is important for nuclear physics and astrophysics.
method: Review of observational data from gravitational-wave events (binary neutron star mergers) and X-ray pulse profile measurements, compared to theoretical nuclear equation of state models.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are presented, showing consistency with some nuclear models but leaving uncertainties at high densities.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine the equation of state, but the paper does not directly address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, testing the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole in the large-scale distribution of matter with the CMB dipole.
motivation: To test the foundational cosmological principle of isotropy and homogeneity by examining a significant inconsistency between the matter dipole and the CMB dipole.
method: Analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole anisotropy and compare it with the CMB dipole, including assessment of biases and systematic issues.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, challenging the standard ΛCDM model.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may indicate a violation of the cosmological principle or require modifications to the standard model of cosmology.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews astrophysical tests of dark matter self-interactions, focusing on dark sector models and their observational signatures.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and test beyond-standard-model physics through astrophysical observations.
method: Review of theoretical models of self-interacting dark matter and comparison with observational data from galaxies to large-scale structures.
result: Summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections and outlines future observational prospects.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable candidate, with ongoing and upcoming surveys expected to provide tighter constraints.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental searches and model constraints.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for physics beyond the Standard Model, but recent experimental results have constrained its parameter space. The paper aims to survey the current status and future discovery potential.
method: The authors review theoretical models and experimental search strategies, and project sensitivities for the High-Luminosity LHC across multiple channels.
result: The paper provides an overview of viable supersymmetric scenarios and estimates of discovery reach for the HL-LHC.
conclusion: Supersymmetry remains viable in certain regions, and the HL-LHC will significantly extend the search sensitivity.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
authors: B. Acharya et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion and helioseismology.
motivation: Understanding hydrogen burning is crucial for predicting stellar luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical and experimental work from the last decade on nuclear reactions, plasma physics, and atomic physics in the solar interior.
result: It provides an updated understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning and its diagnostic probes.
conclusion: The paper advances the model of the solar interior but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the dynamics of gas bubbles in liquids, covering turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes.
motivation: Understanding gas bubble dynamics is crucial for many natural and industrial processes, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The review synthesizes advances over the past 20 years in bubble dynamics, focusing on fluid mechanics.
result: Key insights include the effects of added mass, deformable surfaces, turbulence, and surfactants on bubble behavior.
conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive overview to guide future research in two-phase flow systems, but is unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser pulses to generate ultrasound waves for deep-tissue imaging.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed for biological and clinical insight; optoacoustic imaging offers high-resolution, deep-tissue optical contrast noninvasively.
method: The review covers the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, its impact on biological and clinical research, and recent developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables imaging of optical contrast at millimeter-to-centimeter depths with high resolution, bridging the gap between optical and ultrasound imaging.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological and clinical imaging, with ongoing advancements in multimodal approaches enhancing its capabilities.

title: Broadband High-gain Metalens Design Based On Dispersion Compensation
authors: Yanwei Wang, Chuanfei Li, Zhuo Liu And Yunsheng Guo
abstract: Broadband metasurface focusing is often limited by unit-cell phase dispersion and phase–amplitude coupling, leading to degraded performance near the band edges in conventional geometrical-optics (GO) designs. To address this challenge, an inverse-design method combining an artificial neural network and particle swarm optimization is proposed. The unit-cell response is modeled in the complex domain to avoid phase-wrapping discontinuities, while a frequency-dependent aperture reference phase is globally optimized to balance phase accuracy and transmittance. Based on this method, a broadband metalens operating from 9.0 to 10.2 GHz (12.5%) is designed and fabricated. Measured results agree well with simulations and demonstrate a gain enhancement of up to 4.36 dBi over a conventional GO design, with a peak gain of 23.8 dBi. Compared with the feed antenna alone, the maximum gain improvement reaches 16.05 dBi, while the half-power beamwidth is reduced by up to at 10.2 GHz. The proposed method provides an effective route for broadband high-gain metalens design under practical unit-cell constraints.
tldr: This paper presents an inverse-design method for broadband high-gain metalens using neural network and particle swarm optimization.
motivation: Broadband metasurface focusing is limited by unit-cell phase dispersion and phase-amplitude coupling, degrading performance near band edges in conventional designs.
method: An artificial neural network models the unit-cell response in the complex domain to avoid phase-wrapping discontinuities, and particle swarm optimization globally optimizes a frequency-dependent aperture reference phase.
result: A metalens operating from 9.0 to 10.2 GHz achieves up to 4.36 dBi gain enhancement over conventional design, with peak gain of 23.8 dBi.
conclusion: The proposed method provides an effective route for broadband high-gain metalens design under practical unit-cell constraints.

For two identical atoms with the same world-line, the system reduces to the usual dissipative Dicke model at the first resonant condition where and are the energy splitting and the angular velocity of the th atom, and is the Lorentz factor. The entangled steady-state takes the form where and are constant, which is consistent with the previous study (see 2022 Phys. Rev. D 106 105028). For two atoms with different world-lines, the system suffers from a significant mixed joint dissipation process at the second resonant condition , and reaches an entangled steady-state as . Moreover, with the help of the cavity, we can obtain a much higher concurrence in the final states by changing the relative ratio of the two orbital radii.
